Part I · The Action Principle — Chapter 1.2

Stationary Action

One scalar function, one condition on it, and every equation of motion in this book.

Where we are

Chapter 1.1 ended with a trick that should have unsettled you. To find the path a light ray takes through a stack of media, you did not track the ray. You wrote down a single number for each conceivable path — the total travel time — demanded that this number be stationary, and Snell's law fell out. A global statement about entire paths produced a local law about what happens at one interface.

That is a strange and powerful thing to be able to do, and 1.1 left it as an isolated curiosity about light. This chapter turns it into machinery. We build the branch of mathematics that differentiates a number with respect to a whole function — the calculus of variations — and then point it at mechanics.

Here is the destination, stated up front so you know what you are paying for. There is one scalar function LLL, called the Lagrangian. There is one quantity built from it, S=∫L dtS=\int L\,\dd tS=∫Ldt, called the action. There is one condition, δS=0\delta S=0δS=0. Out of that condition come Newton's laws (§4), the motion of anything with constraints (§6), Maxwell's equations (Chapter 2.6), Einstein's field equations (Chapter 3.6), the Dirac equation (Chapter 5.4), and the Standard Model (Chapter 6.7). Not analogues of them. Them.

This is a mathematics chapter. The physics in §4 onward is there to show you that the mathematics has teeth.

Tools you'll need  — Chapter 0.1: the derivative as the coefficient of the best linear approximation, and the o(h)o(h)o(h) bookkeeping. This chapter is that definition with hhh replaced by an entire function; nothing else changes, which is the whole point of having defined it that way. Chapter 0.2: integration by parts — §3 is one application of it, and the boundary term matters. Chapter 0.6: the multivariable chain rule (§7 is nothing but), stationary points and the Hessian (§5), and Lagrange multipliers (§6.4, where the multiplier turns out to be a physical force). Chapter 1.1: Fermat's principle, and the catalogue of things the force picture cannot do.

1 · Functionals

A function eats a number and returns a number. A functional eats a function and returns a number. That is the entire definition, and the only reason it feels exotic is that you have spent your life with the first kind.

You have in fact been using functionals for years without the word. Here are three, and all three will be doing work before the chapter is out.

Arc length. Given a curve y(x)y(x)y(x) between x=ax=ax=a and x=bx=bx=b, its length is obtained by adding up little hypotenuses ds=dx2+dy2\dd s = \sqrt{\dd x^{2}+\dd y^{2}}ds=dx2+dy2​:

A[y]  =  ∫ab1+y′(x)2  dx. \mathcal{A}[y] \;=\; \int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+y'(x)^{2}}\;\dd x. A[y]=∫ab​1+y′(x)2​dx. (1.2.1)

Fermat's travel time. The same integral, weighted by the local slowness. If light moves at speed c/n(x,y)c/n(x,y)c/n(x,y) where nnn is the refractive index, the time to traverse the curve is

T[y]  =  ∫abn(x,y(x))c 1+y′(x)2  dx. \mathcal{T}[y] \;=\; \int_{a}^{b} \frac{n\big(x,y(x)\big)}{c}\,\sqrt{1+y'(x)^{2}}\;\dd x. T[y]=∫ab​cn(x,y(x))​1+y′(x)2​dx. (1.2.2)

That is exactly the quantity Chapter 1.1 minimised, written out in general instead of for two flat slabs.

The action. Given a trajectory x(t)x(t)x(t) between times t1t_{1}t1​ and t2t_{2}t2​, and given some function L(x,x˙,t)L(x,\dot x,t)L(x,x˙,t) of position, velocity and time,

S[x]  =  ∫t1t2L(x(t),x˙(t),t)  dt. S[x] \;=\; \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} L\big(x(t),\dot x(t),t\big)\;\dd t. S[x]=∫t1​t2​​L(x(t),x˙(t),t)dt. (1.2.3)

We have not yet said what LLL is. That is deliberate; §5 is an honest discussion of where it comes from, and the answer is not what a textbook usually implies. For now LLL is any smooth function of three arguments, and SSS is the functional it defines.

Notice the notation: square brackets. S[x]S[x]S[x] is not "SSS evaluated at the number xxx". It is "SSS evaluated at the function xxx" — you must hand over the entire path, every x(t)x(t)x(t) for every ttt in the interval, before SSS will give you a number back.

The domain is infinite-dimensional, and that is the whole difficulty

To specify a point in R3\R^{3}R3 you supply three numbers. To specify a point in the domain of SSS you supply a value of xxx at every one of a continuum of times. The "variable" of the problem is a path, and the space of paths has infinitely many dimensions — one for each instant, loosely speaking.

So when we go looking for a stationary point of SSS, we are looking for a stationary point of a function on an infinite-dimensional space. Chapter 0.6 found stationary points of f:Rn→Rf:\R^{n}\to\Rf:Rn→R by setting nnn partial derivatives to zero. Here there is no finite list of partial derivatives to set to zero. We will get, instead, one condition per instant of time — which is to say a differential equation. That is the structural reason the answer to a variational problem is always a differential equation, and it is worth seeing before the algebra rather than after.

In plain terms 1.2.1

What is being varied from here on is not a number but an entire history, and the change of type has one consequence worth carrying in advance. A machine that eats a whole function and returns a single number has a domain with infinitely many dimensions, one for each instant, loosely speaking, rather than the three or six that a mechanical problem used to offer.

That is why hunting for a stationary point cannot be done the way it was done on a surface. Finding the flat spot of a function of several variables meant setting a finite list of partial derivatives to zero, and here there is no finite list to set. What comes out instead is one condition for every instant of time, and one condition per instant is a differential equation.

So the answer to a problem of this kind is always a differential equation, for a structural reason rather than as a happy fact about the particular integrals involved. Three such machines are already familiar: the length of a curve, the time light takes along a route, and the quantity that is shortly to be given the whole weight of the subject to carry.

2 · The variational derivative

This section is the conceptual centre of the chapter. Everything after it is consequences.

We want to say what it means for the functional SSS to be stationary at a particular path. The honest difficulty is that we cannot write lim⁡h→0(S[x+h]−S[x])/h\lim_{h\to0}\big(S[x+h]-S[x]\big)/hlimh→0​(S[x+h]−S[x])/h, because the displacement is not a number hhh that we can divide by — it is an entire function. Dividing by a function is not a meaningful operation.

The way out is the one Chapter 0.1 insisted on, at some cost in apparent pedantry, on its first page. The derivative is not a slope. It is the coefficient of the best linear approximation. That definition never mentioned division, and it never mentioned one-dimensionality. It said: nudge the input, and identify the part of the output's response that is linear in the nudge. Nothing about that instruction breaks when the nudge is a function.

2.1 · Reduce to one variable

Fix the path x(t)x(t)x(t) we want to test. Fix a second function η(t)\eta(t)η(t) — the shape of the nudge — subject to one restriction:

η(t1)  =  η(t2)  =  0. \eta(t_{1}) \;=\; \eta(t_{2}) \;=\; 0. η(t1​)=η(t2​)=0. (1.2.4)

Such an η\etaη is called an admissible variation. The restriction says the nudge does not move the endpoints: every path we compare starts at the same place at t1t_{1}t1​ and finishes at the same place at t2t_{2}t2​. That is not a technicality — it is the boundary condition of the physical problem, and in §3 it is precisely what kills a term we would otherwise be stuck with.

Now build a one-parameter family of paths by scaling the nudge:

xϵ(t)  =  x(t)+ϵ η(t),ϵ∈R. x_{\epsilon}(t) \;=\; x(t) + \epsilon\,\eta(t), \qquad \epsilon\in\R. xϵ​(t)=x(t)+ϵη(t),ϵ∈R. (1.2.5)

At ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0 this is the path we are testing; as ϵ\epsilonϵ grows the path bulges away from it in the shape η\etaη, always pinned at both ends. Feed the family into the functional:

Φ(ϵ)  ≡  S[x+ϵη]. \Phi(\epsilon) \;\equiv\; S\big[x+\epsilon\eta\big]. Φ(ϵ)≡S[x+ϵη]. (1.2.6)

Look carefully at what (1.2.6) is. Φ\PhiΦ eats a single real number ϵ\epsilonϵ and returns a single real number. It is an ordinary function of one real variable. All of Chapter 0.1 applies to it verbatim, with no generalisation required at all. We have converted an infinite-dimensional problem into a one-dimensional one by agreeing, for the moment, to look in only one direction.

2.2 · The definition

Say that SSS is stationary at the path xxx if

ddϵS[x+ϵη]∣ϵ=0  =  0for every admissible η. \left.\dv{}{\epsilon}S\big[x+\epsilon\eta\big]\right|_{\epsilon=0} \;=\; 0 \qquad\text{for }\textit{every}\text{ admissible }\eta. dϵd​S[x+ϵη]​ϵ=0​=0for every admissible η. (1.2.7)

The clause in italics is the entire content. Any single η\etaη probes one direction in the space of paths, and a function can easily be stationary along one direction and not others — a saddle is flat along two lines and steep everywhere else. Demanding (1.2.7) for all η\etaη is demanding flatness in every one of the infinitely many available directions at once. That is a very strong condition, and it is strong enough to determine the path.

The quantity in (1.2.7) gets a name and a symbol. Write

δS[x;η]  ≡  ddϵS[x+ϵη]∣ϵ=0, \delta S[x;\eta] \;\equiv\; \left.\dv{}{\epsilon}S\big[x+\epsilon\eta\big]\right|_{\epsilon=0}, δS[x;η]≡dϵd​S[x+ϵη]​ϵ=0​, (1.2.8)

the first variation of SSS at xxx in the direction η\etaη. Unwinding (1.2.8) through Chapter 0.1's definition of a derivative, it is exactly the statement

S[x+ϵη]  =  S[x]⏟value  +  ϵ δS[x;η]⏟linear in the nudge  +  o(ϵ)⏟dies faster. S\big[x+\epsilon\eta\big] \;=\; \underbrace{S[x]}_{\text{value}} \;+\; \underbrace{\epsilon\,\delta S[x;\eta]}_{\text{linear in the nudge}} \;+\; \underbrace{o(\epsilon)}_{\text{dies faster}}. S[x+ϵη]=valueS[x]​​+linear in the nudgeϵδS[x;η]​​+dies fastero(ϵ)​​. (1.2.9)
The cheque written on page one, cashed here

Put (1.2.9) next to Chapter 0.1's central equation,

f(a+h)  =  f(a)+f′(a) h+o(h). f(a+h) \;=\; f(a) + f'(a)\,h + o(h). f(a+h)=f(a)+f′(a)h+o(h).

They are the same sentence. The dictionary is:

Chapter 0.1Here
the point aaathe path x(⋅)x(\cdot)x(⋅)
the displacement hhh, a numberthe variation η(⋅)\eta(\cdot)η(⋅), a whole function
the derivative f′(a)f'(a)f′(a), a numberthe first variation δS[x; ⋅ ]\delta S[x;\,\cdot\,]δS[x;⋅], a linear functional
the linear term f′(a)hf'(a)hf′(a)hthe linear term δS[x;η]\delta S[x;\eta]δS[x;η]
error o(h)o(h)o(h)error o(ϵ)o(\epsilon)o(ϵ)

Had we defined the derivative as "a slope", we would be stuck at the first row. There is no slope of a functional; there is no line to take the slope of, because the domain is a space of paths and there is no single direction to move in. But there is a best linear approximation, and it is unique, and it is what δS\delta SδS names.

Note what kind of object δS[x; ⋅ ]\delta S[x;\,\cdot\,]δS[x;⋅] is. It takes a function η\etaη and returns a number, and it does so linearly: δS[x;αη1+βη2]=α δS[x;η1]+β δS[x;η2]\delta S[x;\alpha\eta_{1}+\beta\eta_{2}] = \alpha\,\delta S[x;\eta_{1}] + \beta\,\delta S[x;\eta_{2}]δS[x;αη1​+βη2​]=αδS[x;η1​]+βδS[x;η2​], which you can read straight off (1.2.8) once §3 has computed it. A linear map whose target is R\RR (Chapter 0.4) is what Chapter 0.6 called a linear functional, and, in finite dimensions, a one-form or covector. The derivative of a functional is a one-form on the space of paths — which is why it is written with a lower index in disguise, as the coefficient against which you integrate. That sentence will be true word for word in Chapter 5.5, with the path replaced by a field configuration.

2.3 · The functional derivative

One more piece of notation, because physics uses it constantly and it is easy to be mystified by it. In finite dimensions, Chapter 0.6 wrote the derivative of f:Rn→Rf:\R^{n}\to\Rf:Rn→R in the direction h\vv hh as a sum over components,

df(h)  =  ∑i=1n∂f∂xi hi. \dd f(\vv h) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{n}\pdv{f}{x^{i}}\,h^{i}. df(h)=i=1∑n​∂xi∂f​hi. (1.2.10)

The gradient components ∂f/∂xi\partial f/\partial x^{i}∂f/∂xi are the coefficients of the linear map, one per direction. Here the directions are labelled not by an index iii running over 1,…,n1,\dots,n1,…,n but by a time ttt running over [t1,t2][t_{1},t_{2}][t1​,t2​], and the sum over the label becomes an integral over it. So we define the functional derivative δS/δx(t)\delta S/\delta x(t)δS/δx(t) to be the coefficient function appearing in

δS[x;η]  =  ∫t1t2δSδx(t)  η(t)  dt. \delta S[x;\eta] \;=\; \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} \frac{\delta S}{\delta x(t)}\;\eta(t)\;\dd t. δS[x;η]=∫t1​t2​​δx(t)δS​η(t)dt. (1.2.11)

Compare (1.2.11) with (1.2.10): index →\to→ time, sum →\to→ integral, gradient component →\to→ functional derivative. It is a continuum gradient. Section 3 is going to compute it, and the answer will be the Euler–Lagrange expression; the condition δS=0\delta S=0δS=0 for all η\etaη will then become the statement that this continuum gradient vanishes at every ttt, which is one equation per instant, as promised.

In plain terms 1.2.2

Dividing by a function is not an operation, so the picture of a derivative as one change divided by another has nowhere to stand here. The definition that does stand is the one insisted on at the very start of the toolkit, at some cost in apparent fussiness: nudge the input, and identify the part of the response that is linear in the nudge. Nothing in that instruction cares whether the nudge is a small number or a whole function.

So the pedantry of the opening pages is repaid a second time, and for far more than it was repaid the first. Several variables cost only the replacement of one direction by many; here the displacement is an entire function, and the coefficient is no longer a number but a device that eats such functions and returns numbers. The error still dies faster than the nudge, and everything else is unchanged word for word.

The demand being made is stronger than it looks. Any single choice of nudge probes one direction in the space of paths, and something can easily be flat along one direction while falling away steeply in others. Requiring flatness against every admissible nudge at once is requiring it in infinitely many directions simultaneously, and that is what makes the condition strong enough to pick out one path.

3 · Euler–Lagrange, derived

Now do the calculation. Take S[x]=∫t1t2L(x,x˙,t) dtS[x]=\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}L(x,\dot x,t)\,\dd tS[x]=∫t1​t2​​L(x,x˙,t)dt with LLL smooth, and compute δS\delta SδS. There are exactly four moves, and you have all four already.

3.1 · Move one: differentiate under the integral sign

Write out Φ(ϵ)\Phi(\epsilon)Φ(ϵ). Since xϵ=x+ϵηx_{\epsilon}=x+\epsilon\etaxϵ​=x+ϵη implies x˙ϵ=x˙+ϵη˙\dot x_{\epsilon}=\dot x+\epsilon\dot\etax˙ϵ​=x˙+ϵη˙​,

Φ(ϵ)  =  ∫t1t2L(x+ϵη,  x˙+ϵη˙,  t) dt. \Phi(\epsilon) \;=\; \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} L\big(x+\epsilon\eta,\;\dot x+\epsilon\dot\eta,\;t\big)\,\dd t. Φ(ϵ)=∫t1​t2​​L(x+ϵη,x˙+ϵη˙​,t)dt. (1.2.12)

We want Φ′(0)\Phi'(0)Φ′(0). The integrand depends on ϵ\epsilonϵ; the limits do not. Assume for the moment that we may move the ϵ\epsilonϵ-derivative inside:

dΦdϵ  =  ∫t1t2∂∂ϵ L(x+ϵη,  x˙+ϵη˙,  t) dt. \dv{\Phi}{\epsilon} \;=\; \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} \pdv{}{\epsilon}\,L\big(x+\epsilon\eta,\;\dot x+\epsilon\dot\eta,\;t\big)\,\dd t. dϵdΦ​=∫t1​t2​​∂ϵ∂​L(x+ϵη,x˙+ϵη˙​,t)dt. (1.2.13)

⚑ Quoted. The interchange in (1.2.13) is the one step in this derivation we are not proving. The standard sufficient condition is: if LLL and its ϵ\epsilonϵ-partial derivative are continuous on the rectangle [t1,t2]×[−ϵ0,ϵ0][t_{1},t_{2}]\times[-\epsilon_{0},\epsilon_{0}][t1​,t2​]×[−ϵ0​,ϵ0​], then Φ\PhiΦ is differentiable and (1.2.13) holds. Since we are assuming LLL is a smooth function of its three arguments and x,ηx,\etax,η are smooth on a closed bounded interval, that condition is met. The grind box below says what can go wrong when it is not.

3.2 · Move two: linearise the integrand

The ϵ\epsilonϵ-derivative inside is the multivariable chain rule of Chapter 0.6, applied to LLL as a function of its first two slots. Write ∂L/∂x\partial L/\partial x∂L/∂x and ∂L/∂x˙\partial L/\partial\dot x∂L/∂x˙ for the partial derivatives of LLL with respect to its first and second arguments. Then, since the first argument moves at rate η\etaη and the second at rate η˙\dot\etaη˙​ as ϵ\epsilonϵ increases,

∂∂ϵL(x+ϵη,x˙+ϵη˙,t)  =  ∂L∂x η  +  ∂L∂x˙ η˙, \pdv{}{\epsilon}L\big(x+\epsilon\eta,\dot x+\epsilon\dot\eta,t\big) \;=\; \pdv{L}{x}\,\eta \;+\; \pdv{L}{\dot x}\,\dot\eta, ∂ϵ∂​L(x+ϵη,x˙+ϵη˙​,t)=∂x∂L​η+∂x˙∂L​η˙​, (1.2.14)

where after setting ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0 the partials are evaluated on the original path (x(t),x˙(t),t)\big(x(t),\dot x(t),t\big)(x(t),x˙(t),t). So

δS  =  ∫t1t2[∂L∂x η(t)  +  ∂L∂x˙ η˙(t)]dt. \delta S \;=\; \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left[\pdv{L}{x}\,\eta(t) \;+\; \pdv{L}{\dot x}\,\dot\eta(t)\right]\dd t. δS=∫t1​t2​​[∂x∂L​η(t)+∂x˙∂L​η˙​(t)]dt. (1.2.15)

We are stuck, and it is worth being precise about why. To conclude anything about the integrand we need η\etaη to appear as an overall factor, so that "this holds for every η\etaη" has bite. It does in the first term. In the second term what appears is η˙\dot\etaη˙​, which is not independent of η\etaη — it is determined by it. We cannot choose them separately, so we cannot argue term by term.

3.3 · Move three: integrate by parts

This is exactly the situation Chapter 0.2 built integration by parts for: you may move a derivative from one factor onto the other, at the cost of a minus sign and a boundary term. Apply it to the second term with u=∂L/∂x˙u = \partial L/\partial\dot xu=∂L/∂x˙ and v′=η˙v'=\dot\etav′=η˙​, so v=ηv=\etav=η:

∫t1t2∂L∂x˙ η˙  dt  =  [∂L∂x˙ η]t1t2  −  ∫t1t2ddt ⁣(∂L∂x˙)η  dt. \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\pdv{L}{\dot x}\,\dot\eta\;\dd t \;=\; \left[\pdv{L}{\dot x}\,\eta\right]_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} \;-\; \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{L}{\dot x}\right)\eta\;\dd t. ∫t1​t2​​∂x˙∂L​η˙​dt=[∂x˙∂L​η]t1​t2​​−∫t1​t2​​dtd​(∂x˙∂L​)ηdt. (1.2.16)

Now look at the boundary term. It is (∂L/∂x˙)∣t2η(t2)−(∂L/∂x˙)∣t1η(t1)\big(\partial L/\partial\dot x\big)\big|_{t_{2}}\eta(t_{2}) - \big(\partial L/\partial\dot x\big)\big|_{t_{1}}\eta(t_{1})(∂L/∂x˙)​t2​​η(t2​)−(∂L/∂x˙)​t1​​η(t1​), and by (1.2.4) — the requirement that admissible variations vanish at the endpoints — both η\etaη's are zero. The boundary term dies.

It dies because we fixed the endpoints, not because of any property of LLL. That is worth remembering rather than deriving twice, because when you eventually stop fixing the endpoints — which happens in Chapter 1.3, in Chapter 3.6 for gravity, and everywhere in field theory where the "boundary" is at spatial infinity — the surviving boundary term is not litter. It is where the momentum lives, and where the black-hole entropy will come from.

Substituting (1.2.16) into (1.2.15) and collecting the common factor η\etaη:

δS  =  ∫t1t2[∂L∂x  −  ddt ⁣(∂L∂x˙)]η(t)  dt. \delta S \;=\; \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left[\pdv{L}{x} \;-\; \dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{L}{\dot x}\right)\right]\eta(t)\;\dd t. δS=∫t1​t2​​[∂x∂L​−dtd​(∂x˙∂L​)]η(t)dt. (1.2.17)

Compare with (1.2.11) and read off the answer to §2.3: the functional derivative of the action is the bracket,

δSδx(t)  =  ∂L∂x  −  ddt ⁣(∂L∂x˙). \frac{\delta S}{\delta x(t)} \;=\; \pdv{L}{x} \;-\; \dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{L}{\dot x}\right). δx(t)δS​=∂x∂L​−dtd​(∂x˙∂L​). (1.2.18)

3.4 · Move four: the fundamental lemma

Stationarity says (1.2.17) vanishes for every admissible η\etaη. We want to conclude that the bracket vanishes. That step is not free — it is a genuine theorem, and skipping it is skipping the move that converts "the integral is zero" into "the integrand is zero". The same move recurs in Chapter 5.2 to produce field equations and in Chapter 3.6 to produce Einstein's, so we prove it once, here, properly.

Fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations

Let fff be continuous on [t1,t2][t_{1},t_{2}][t1​,t2​]. If

∫t1t2f(t) η(t) dt  =  0 \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}} f(t)\,\eta(t)\,\dd t \;=\; 0 ∫t1​t2​​f(t)η(t)dt=0

for every continuously differentiable η\etaη with η(t1)=η(t2)=0\eta(t_{1})=\eta(t_{2})=0η(t1​)=η(t2​)=0, then f(t)=0f(t)=0f(t)=0 for all t∈[t1,t2]t\in[t_{1},t_{2}]t∈[t1​,t2​].

The theorem is not obvious and it is not trivially true. An integral can vanish through cancellation — ∫−11t dt=0\int_{-1}^{1}t\,\dd t=0∫−11​tdt=0 without ttt being zero anywhere but the origin. The hypothesis defeats cancellation by allowing you to choose η\etaη: if fff is positive somewhere, pick an η\etaη that is supported only there, and there is nothing left to cancel against. Making that idea airtight requires exhibiting such an η\etaη, which is the content of the proof.

Proof. Suppose, for contradiction, that fff is not identically zero. Then there is a point t0t_{0}t0​ with f(t0)≠0f(t_{0})\neq0f(t0​)=0; replacing fff by −f-f−f if necessary (which changes nothing, since the hypothesis is preserved), assume f(t0)>0f(t_{0}) \gt 0f(t0​)>0. If t0t_{0}t0​ is an endpoint, continuity gives a nearby interior point where fff is still positive, so assume t0t_{0}t0​ is interior.

3.5 · The Euler–Lagrange equation

Apply the lemma to (1.2.17). The bracket is continuous (we assumed LLL smooth and the path smooth), and the integral vanishes for every admissible η\etaη. Therefore the bracket vanishes identically, and we have

  ddt ⁣(∂L∂x˙)  −  ∂L∂x  =  0   \boxed{\;\dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{L}{\dot x}\right) \;-\; \pdv{L}{x} \;=\; 0\;} dtd​(∂x˙∂L​)−∂x∂L​=0​ (1.2.22)

for all t∈[t1,t2]t\in[t_{1},t_{2}]t∈[t1​,t2​]. This is the Euler–Lagrange equation. It is a second-order ordinary differential equation for x(t)x(t)x(t) — second order because ∂L/∂x˙\partial L/\partial\dot x∂L/∂x˙ depends on x˙\dot xx˙, and differentiating it in time produces x¨\ddot xx¨. Two constants of integration, fixed by the two endpoint conditions. Everything is consistent.

Nothing in the derivation used the fact that there was one coordinate. Suppose the configuration is described by nnn numbers q1,…,qnq^{1},\dots,q^{n}q1,…,qn and L=L(q1,…,qn,q˙1,…,q˙n,t)L=L(q^{1},\dots,q^{n},\dot q^{1},\dots,\dot q^{n},t)L=L(q1,…,qn,q˙​1,…,q˙​n,t). Move two produces ∑i[∂qiL ηi+∂q˙iL η˙i]\sum_{i}\big[\partial_{q^{i}}L\,\eta^{i} + \partial_{\dot q^{i}}L\,\dot\eta^{i}\big]∑i​[∂qi​Lηi+∂q˙​i​Lη˙​i], move three integrates each term by parts separately, and move four is applied nnn times — once with η1\eta^{1}η1 arbitrary and all other ηi=0\eta^{i}=0ηi=0, once with η2\eta^{2}η2 arbitrary, and so on. The result is

ddt ⁣(∂L∂q˙i)−∂L∂qi  =  0,i=1,…,n. \dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}}\right) - \pdv{L}{q^{i}} \;=\; 0, \qquad i=1,\dots,n. dtd​(∂q˙​i∂L​)−∂qi∂L​=0,i=1,…,n. (1.2.23)

One equation per degree of freedom, all of them from the single scalar LLL. That compression — nnn coupled second-order differential equations packaged in one function — is the first practical reason to care, and by §6 it will look like a bargain.

There are now two boundary terms, and killing them needs both η\etaη and η˙\dot\etaη˙​ to vanish at the ends — which is to say the variational problem is only well posed if you fix the position and the velocity at each endpoint. Given that, the fundamental lemma applies verbatim and delivers

∂F∂q−ddt ⁣(∂F∂q˙)+d2dt2 ⁣(∂F∂q¨)=0, \pdv{F}{q} - \dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{F}{\dot q}\right) + \dv{^{2}}{t^{2}}\!\left(\pdv{F}{\ddot q}\right) = 0, ∂q∂F​−dtd​(∂q˙​∂F​)+dt2d2​(∂q¨​∂F​)=0,

⚑ One quoted warning, because it explains an omission you will otherwise notice. Ostrogradsky proved that a Lagrangian genuinely depending on q¨\ddot qq¨​ has a conserved energy that is linear in one of its momenta and therefore unbounded below — such theories are generically unstable. That is why every fundamental action in §8.1's table contains at most first derivatives of its fields. The Einstein–Hilbert action looks like an exception, since RRR contains second derivatives of the metric; it escapes because those second derivatives enter only inside a total divergence, as Chapter 3.6 will show explicitly.

In plain terms 1.2.3

The calculation producing the equation of motion is short, and nearly all of its load is carried by one manoeuvre borrowed from the chapter on integration. Once the nudge is inside the integrand, one term carries it as a plain factor and the other carries its rate of change, and the two cannot be argued about separately because the second is determined by the first. Moving the derivative off one factor and onto the other repairs that, at the cost of a sign and a term evaluated only at the two ends.

This is exactly the use advertised for integration by parts several chapters back, the step converting a statement about one whole total into an equation the system must satisfy at every point, which is where every field equation in this book comes from. The end term dies because the endpoints were held fixed and not because of any property of the integrand, worth remembering for the occasions when the ends are free and the surviving term turns out to be where the momentum lives.

One step remains and it is not free. An integral can vanish through cancellation without its integrand vanishing anywhere, and what defeats the cancellation is that the nudge is yours to choose, so you may aim a small bump wherever the integrand is not zero and leave it nothing to cancel against.

4 · It reproduces Newton

Time to check that this machinery is not describing some other universe. Take a single particle of mass mmm moving in one dimension in a potential V(x)V(x)V(x), and make the choice

L  =  T−V  =  12mx˙2  −  V(x). L \;=\; T - V \;=\; \half m\dot x^{2} \;-\; V(x). L=T−V=21​mx˙2−V(x). (1.2.24)

Where that choice comes from is §5's problem. Right now we only want its consequences. Compute the two partial derivatives, treating xxx and x˙\dot xx˙ as independent slots of the function LLL — which is legitimate for the reason spelled out in the warning callout below:

∂L∂x˙  =  mx˙,∂L∂x  =  − dVdx. \pdv{L}{\dot x} \;=\; m\dot x, \qquad\qquad \pdv{L}{x} \;=\; -\,\dv{V}{x}. ∂x˙∂L​=mx˙,∂x∂L​=−dxdV​. (1.2.25)

Substitute into (1.2.22):

ddt(mx˙)+dVdx=0⟺mx¨  =  −dVdx. \dv{}{t}\big(m\dot x\big) + \dv{V}{x} = 0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad m\ddot x \;=\; -\dv{V}{x}. dtd​(mx˙)+dxdV​=0⟺mx¨=−dxdV​. (1.2.26)

The right-hand side is the force, by Chapter 1.1's definition of a conservative force as minus the gradient of its potential. So (1.2.26) is mx¨=Fm\ddot x = Fmx¨=F.

In three dimensions nothing changes except the number of equations. With L=12m x˙⋅x˙−V(x)L=\half m\,\dot{\vv x}\cdot\dot{\vv x} - V(\vv x)L=21​mx˙⋅x˙−V(x) and qi=xiq^{i}=x^{i}qi=xi,

∂L∂x˙i=mx˙i,∂L∂xi=−∂V∂xi,⟹mx¨i=−∂V∂xi=Fi. \pdv{L}{\dot x^{i}} = m\dot x^{i}, \qquad \pdv{L}{x^{i}} = -\pdv{V}{x^{i}}, \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad m\ddot x^{i} = -\pdv{V}{x^{i}} = F^{i}. ∂x˙i∂L​=mx˙i,∂xi∂L​=−∂xi∂V​,⟹mx¨i=−∂xi∂V​=Fi. (1.2.27)

Now read (1.2.27) again, slowly, without substituting anything. The object ∂L/∂x˙i\partial L/\partial\dot x^{i}∂L/∂x˙i turned out to be mx˙im\dot x^{i}mx˙i — the momentum. The object ∂L/∂xi\partial L/\partial x^{i}∂L/∂xi turned out to be −∂V/∂xi-\partial V/\partial x^{i}−∂V/∂xi — the force. So the Euler–Lagrange equation, in Cartesian coordinates with L=T−VL=T-VL=T−V, reads

dpidt  =  Fi. \dv{p_{i}}{t} \;=\; F_{i}. dtdpi​​=Fi​. (1.2.28)

Newton's second law is not a separate law that happens to agree with the action principle. It is the Euler–Lagrange equation, written in Cartesian coordinates. That is the entire relationship between Chapter 1.1 and this one.

This also explains why the notation generalises the way it does. For an arbitrary Lagrangian and arbitrary coordinates we define

pi  ≡  ∂L∂q˙i(the canonical momentum conjugate to qi), p_{i} \;\equiv\; \pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}} \qquad (\text{the }\textit{canonical momentum}\text{ conjugate to }q^{i}), pi​≡∂q˙​i∂L​(the canonical momentum conjugate to qi), (1.2.29)

whereupon (1.2.23) always reads p˙i=∂L/∂qi\dot p_{i} = \partial L/\partial q^{i}p˙​i​=∂L/∂qi. The definition is not a whim: it is chosen so that the Euler–Lagrange equation keeps the shape of Newton's law. Chapter 1.3 takes pip_{i}pi​ seriously as an independent variable and gets Hamiltonian mechanics; Chapter 1.4 shows that whenever LLL fails to depend on some qiq^{i}qi at all, the corresponding pip_{i}pi​ is conserved — which is Noether's theorem in its simplest guise, already visible in (1.2.23) for anyone who looks.

⚠ Why this isn't obvious

In (1.2.25) we differentiated LLL with respect to x˙\dot xx˙ while holding xxx fixed. That should bother you. Along an actual trajectory x˙\dot xx˙ is not free to vary independently of xxx — it is xxx's own derivative. Holding one fixed while changing the other looks like nonsense.

The resolution is to be careful about what LLL is a function of. LLL is a function of three independent arguments — call them (u,v,t)(u,v,t)(u,v,t) — defined on a space of its own, with no relationship between uuu and vvv whatsoever. For the free particle, L(u,v,t)=12mv2−V(u)L(u,v,t)=\half mv^{2}-V(u)L(u,v,t)=21​mv2−V(u) is defined for every pair (u,v)∈R2(u,v)\in\R^{2}(u,v)∈R2, and ∂L/∂v=mv\partial L/\partial v = mv∂L/∂v=mv is a perfectly ordinary partial derivative of that perfectly ordinary function of two variables. The constraint "vvv is the time derivative of uuu" is imposed only when you evaluate: the action (1.2.3) substitutes u=x(t)u=x(t)u=x(t) and v=x˙(t)v=\dot x(t)v=x˙(t) into LLL after the partial derivatives have been taken.

The precise statement is that LLL is a function on the tangent bundle of the configuration space — the space whose points are (position, velocity) pairs, with both free. A path in configuration space lifts to a curve in the tangent bundle by attaching to each point its own velocity, and that lift is where the constraint lives. Chapter 3.2 constructs the tangent bundle properly; for now the operational rule is exact and safe: differentiate LLL symbolically, treating xxx and x˙\dot xx˙ as unrelated letters; only afterwards put the path in. The ddt\dv{}{t}dtd​ in (1.2.22) is the one operation that does know about the path — it is a total time derivative along the trajectory, and it is why ddt(∂L/∂x˙)\dv{}{t}\big(\partial L/\partial\dot x\big)dtd​(∂L/∂x˙) generates x¨\ddot xx¨ terms while ∂L/∂x˙\partial L/\partial\dot x∂L/∂x˙ alone does not.

In plain terms 1.2.4

Newton's second law is not a rival to the new machinery, nor a separate law that happens to agree with it. It is the same equation, written in one coordinate system with one choice of the scalar, and that choice is the kinetic energy less the potential energy. Turn the crank and the two objects appearing are the momentum and the force, in that order and in those roles.

That reading licenses the definition carried forward from here. Whatever the scalar yields when differentiated with respect to a velocity is thereafter the momentum conjugate to that coordinate, and the equation always says its rate of change equals the derivative of the scalar with respect to the coordinate itself. The name is not sentimental. It is chosen so that the equation keeps Newton's shape whatever the coordinates happen to be, and the payoff shows immediately: where a coordinate fails to appear in the scalar at all, its conjugate momentum cannot change.

One habit here deserves a warning. Position and velocity are differentiated as though they were unrelated letters, which along an actual trajectory they are not. The resolution is that the scalar is defined on a space where they genuinely are unrelated, and their relation is imposed only afterwards, when a path is substituted in.

5 · Why T−VT-VT−V? An honest answer

You have just watched L=T−VL=T-VL=T−V reproduce Newtonian mechanics exactly. The natural next question is where T−VT-VT−V came from, and the honest answer has three parts, of which only the third is satisfying.

Part one: within classical mechanics, it is not derived. There is no argument that starts from Newton's laws and ends at L=T−VL=T-VL=T−V by necessity. What there is, is the calculation of §4 run backwards: if you want a variational principle whose Euler–Lagrange equation is mx¨=−V′(x)m\ddot x=-V'(x)mx¨=−V′(x), then 12mx˙2−V(x)\half m\dot x^{2}-V(x)21​mx˙2−V(x) is a Lagrangian that does the job. It is not the only one — §"Your turn" Problem 4 shows you may add any total time derivative without changing a thing, and multiplying LLL by a nonzero constant also leaves the equations alone. T−VT-VT−V is a choice, justified after the fact by the fact that it works. Anyone who tells you the minus sign is intuitive is selling something.

Part two: "least action" is the wrong word. The condition we imposed, (1.2.7), is that the first variation vanishes. That is stationarity, exactly as in Chapter 0.6 — and Chapter 0.6 was emphatic that a vanishing gradient signals a maximum, a minimum, or a saddle, and that in more than one dimension saddles are the generic case. The space of paths has infinitely many dimensions. Saddles are not the exception there; they are ordinary. The warning callout below makes this concrete with a system where the action is provably not a minimum.

Part three: the real reason, which is quantum. In Chapter 5.8 we will construct the Feynman path integral, in which a quantum particle going from AAA to BBB contributes an amplitude from every path, each weighted by the phase

e iS[x]/ℏ. \ee^{\,\ii S[x]/\hbar}. eiS[x]/ℏ. (1.2.30)

The total amplitude is the sum over all paths. Now consider what that sum does. Away from a stationary point of SSS, neighbouring paths have actions differing at first order in the separation, so their phases differ at first order too; since ℏ\hbarℏ is tiny, S/ℏS/\hbarS/ℏ swings through many multiples of 2π2\pi2π over a microscopic change of path, and the contributions from neighbouring paths point in every direction on the complex plane and cancel. Near a stationary point, by construction, SSS changes only at second order — a whole neighbourhood of paths shares essentially the same phase, and their contributions add rather than cancel.

So the classical path is not selected because nature computes an integral and minimises it. Nature does not extremise anything. The classical path is simply where the quantum amplitudes fail to cancel. The action principle is a statement about constructive interference that survives into the ℏ→0\hbar\to0ℏ→0 limit, and the reason the classical path is the stationary one is that stationary phase is the only place a wildly oscillating sum can leave a residue. The reason L=T−VL=T-VL=T−V and not something else is then pushed back one level: it is whatever sits in the exponent of the quantum theory, and that gets fixed in Chapter 5.3 by symmetry requirements — Lorentz invariance, locality, and the demand that the theory be unitary.

⚑ That paragraph is a promise, not a derivation. Nothing in it is proved here; it is stated so that you know a real explanation exists and where it is, and so that you do not spend the next six chapters believing that "nature is economical" is an explanation. It isn't. Chapter 5.8 redeems the promise, including the stationary-phase approximation that makes "wildly oscillating integrals localise on stationary points" a theorem rather than a story.

5.1 · Seeing stationarity

Before the abstractions pile up, look at the thing itself. The figure below takes the simplest system with a curved trajectory — a particle thrown straight up in uniform gravity — and lets you deform its path while watching the action.

The setup: mass m=1 kgm=1\ \mathrm{kg}m=1 kg, gravity g=9.8 m s−2g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}g=9.8 ms−2, and a path that starts at y=0y=0y=0 at t=0t=0t=0 and returns to y=0y=0y=0 at t=T=1 st=T=1\ \mathrm{s}t=T=1 s. The Euler–Lagrange equation (1.2.26) with V=mgyV=mgyV=mgy gives y¨=−g\ddot y=-gy¨​=−g, whose solution with those endpoints is the parabola y∗(t)=12g t(T−t)y_{\ast}(t)=\tfrac12 g\,t(T-t)y∗​(t)=21​gt(T−t), peaking at 1.225 m1.225\ \mathrm{m}1.225 m. Its action, worked out directly,

⚠ Why this isn't obvious

The principle is called "least action" and the quantity is very often not least. Here is a system where you can prove it in four lines.

Take the harmonic oscillator, L=12mx˙2−12mω2x2L = \half m\dot x^{2}-\half m\omega^{2}x^{2}L=21​mx˙2−21​mω2x2, and the path x∗(t)≡0x_{\ast}(t)\equiv0x∗​(t)≡0 on [0,T][0,\mathcal{T}][0,T], which satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation x¨=−ω2x\ddot x=-\omega^{2}xx¨=−ω2x and both endpoint conditions x(0)=x(T)=0x(0)=x(\mathcal{T})=0x(0)=x(T)=0. Since LLL is exactly quadratic, the expansion again terminates, and since the first variation vanishes,

ΔS=m2∫0T(η˙2−ω2η2)dt. \Delta S = \frac{m}{2}\int_{0}^{\mathcal{T}}\big(\dot\eta^{2}-\omega^{2}\eta^{2}\big)\dd t. ΔS=2m​∫0T​(η˙​2−ω2η2)dt.

Choose the admissible variation η=Asin⁡(πt/T)\eta = A\sin(\pi t/\mathcal{T})η=Asin(πt/T). Using ∫0Tsin⁡2(πt/T)dt=∫0Tcos⁡2(πt/T)dt=T/2\int_{0}^{\mathcal{T}}\sin^{2}(\pi t/\mathcal{T})\dd t = \int_{0}^{\mathcal{T}}\cos^{2}(\pi t/\mathcal{T})\dd t = \mathcal{T}/2∫0T​sin2(πt/T)dt=∫0T​cos2(πt/T)dt=T/2,

ΔS=mA2T4[(πT)2−ω2]. \Delta S = \frac{m A^{2}\mathcal{T}}{4}\left[\left(\frac{\pi}{\mathcal{T}}\right)^{2} - \omega^{2}\right]. ΔS=4mA2T​[(Tπ​)2−ω2].

For T<π/ω\mathcal{T} \lt \pi/\omegaT<π/ω this is positive and the stationary path is a minimum. For T>π/ω\mathcal{T} \gt \pi/\omegaT>π/ω — a trip lasting longer than half a period — it is negative: we have exhibited a nearby path with strictly smaller action. The stationary path is a saddle. Nothing has gone wrong; δS=0\delta S=0δS=0 still holds, and the equation of motion is still right. "Least" was simply never the claim.

The instant T=π/ω\mathcal{T}=\pi/\omegaT=π/ω at which the minimum is lost is called a conjugate point: the time at which a second solution with the same endpoints first appears (here, the oscillator can start at the origin, swing out, and return exactly half a period later). ⚑ The general theory — Jacobi's theorem, that the second variation is positive definite precisely up to the first conjugate point — is quoted, not proved. The clean geometric example is on a sphere: both arcs of a great circle joining two cities satisfy the geodesic equation, and the long way round is a perfectly good stationary point of arc length that is emphatically not the shortest path. In Chapter 3.7 those two arcs become the two images of a gravitationally lensed quasar, and the conjugate point becomes the caustic.

Grind box — the second variation in general, and the one condition you can check by eye

The oscillator's ΔS\Delta SΔS was exact because its LLL was quadratic. In general it is only the leading correction, and getting it is Chapter 0.6's second-order Taylor expansion applied to Φ(ϵ)=S[x+ϵη]\Phi(\epsilon)=S[x+\epsilon\eta]Φ(ϵ)=S[x+ϵη]. Differentiate (1.2.15) once more in ϵ\epsilonϵ and set ϵ=0\epsilon=0ϵ=0:

δ2S  ≡  Φ′′(0)  =  ∫t1t2 ⁣[∂2L∂x2η2+2 ∂2L∂x ∂x˙ ηη˙+∂2L∂x˙2η˙2]dt, \delta^{2}S \;\equiv\; \Phi''(0) \;=\; \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\!\left[\pdv{^{2}L}{x^{2}}\eta^{2} + 2\,\frac{\partial^{2}L}{\partial x\,\partial\dot x}\,\eta\dot\eta + \pdv{^{2}L}{\dot x^{2}}\dot\eta^{2}\right]\dd t, δ2S≡Φ′′(0)=∫t1​t2​​[∂x2∂2L​η2+2∂x∂x˙∂2L​ηη˙​+∂x˙2∂2L​η˙​2]dt,

so that S[x+ϵη]=S[x]+ϵ δS+12ϵ2 δ2S+o(ϵ2)S[x+\epsilon\eta] = S[x] + \epsilon\,\delta S + \tfrac12\epsilon^{2}\,\delta^{2}S + o(\epsilon^{2})S[x+ϵη]=S[x]+ϵδS+21​ϵ2δ2S+o(ϵ2). This is exactly Chapter 0.6's Hessian, with the matrix replaced by an integral kernel. Tidy it using 2ηη˙=ddt(η2)2\eta\dot\eta = \dv{}{t}(\eta^{2})2ηη˙​=dtd​(η2) and one integration by parts, whose boundary term dies as usual:

δ2S=∫t1t2[P(t) η˙2+Q(t) η2]dt,P=∂2L∂x˙2,Q=∂2L∂x2−ddt ⁣(∂2L∂x ∂x˙). \delta^{2}S = \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\Big[P(t)\,\dot\eta^{2} + Q(t)\,\eta^{2}\Big]\dd t, \qquad P = \pdv{^{2}L}{\dot x^{2}}, \quad Q = \pdv{^{2}L}{x^{2}} - \dv{}{t}\!\left(\frac{\partial^{2}L}{\partial x\,\partial \dot x}\right). δ2S=∫t1​t2​​[P(t)η˙​2+Q(t)η2]dt,P=∂x˙2∂2L​,Q=∂x2∂2L​−dtd​(∂x∂x˙∂2L​).

The condition you can check by eye. A minimum requires P(t)≥0P(t)\ge0P(t)≥0 everywhere along the path. The argument is the reason fast wiggles matter: take η\etaη to be a tiny bump of height AAA concentrated in a window of width www around a point where P<0P \lt 0P<0. Then ∫Qη2∼A2w\int Q\eta^{2}\sim A^{2}w∫Qη2∼A2w while ∫Pη˙2∼PA2/w\int P\dot\eta^{2}\sim P A^{2}/w∫Pη˙​2∼PA2/w, so shrinking www makes the PPP term dominate with whatever sign PPP has. If P<0P \lt 0P<0 anywhere, δ2S\delta^{2}Sδ2S can be made as negative as you like — no minimum. This is the Legendre condition, and for L=T−VL=T-VL=T−V it reads P=m>0P=m \gt 0P=m>0, satisfied automatically.

It is also worth checking on the one action in §8.1's table you can already differentiate. Chapter 2.5's free relativistic particle has L=−mc21−x˙2/c2L=-mc^{2}\sqrt{1-\dot x^{2}/c^{2}}L=−mc21−x˙2/c2​, giving ∂L/∂x˙=γmx˙\partial L/\partial\dot x = \gamma m\dot x∂L/∂x˙=γmx˙ and P=∂2L/∂x˙2=mγ3>0P = \partial^{2}L/\partial\dot x^{2} = m\gamma^{3} \gt 0P=∂2L/∂x˙2=mγ3>0. So SSS is minimised — and since S=−mc2 ⁣∫dτS=-mc^{2}\!\int\dd\tauS=−mc2∫dτ is minus the proper time, minimising SSS means maximising the proper time along the worldline. The minus sign in front of mc2mc^{2}mc2 is there precisely to arrange that, and it is why the travelling twin, who takes a non-extremal path, comes back younger.

⚑ Legendre's condition is necessary, not sufficient. The sufficient statement — Jacobi's theorem, that δ2S>0\delta^{2}S \gt 0δ2S>0 for all nonzero admissible η\etaη precisely when P>0P \gt 0P>0 and the interval contains no conjugate point — is quoted here and not proved; it is a boundary-value problem for the equation ddt(Pu˙)−Qu=0\dv{}{t}(P\dot u) - Qu = 0dtd​(Pu˙)−Qu=0, whose zeros are the conjugate points. For the oscillator, P=mP=mP=m, Q=−mω2Q=-m\omega^{2}Q=−mω2, that equation is u¨=−ω2u\ddot u = -\omega^{2}uu¨=−ω2u, its solution starting at u(0)=0u(0)=0u(0)=0 is sin⁡ωt\sin\omega tsinωt, and its next zero is at t=π/ωt=\pi/\omegat=π/ω — exactly the half-period the callout found by exhibiting a variation. The general theory reproduces the special case, which is the least one can ask of it.

In plain terms 1.2.5

Where the combination of kinetic minus potential comes from is the question this chapter refuses to dodge, and the honest answer has a hole. Within classical physics no argument begins at Newton's laws and arrives at that combination by necessity. There is the observation that it works, and the knowledge that it is not the only thing that would: adding anything itself a rate of change, or multiplying the whole by a constant, leaves every prediction untouched. The minus sign is not intuitive and nobody should pretend otherwise.

A second correction concerns the word least, wrong since the principle was named. The condition imposed is that the first-order change vanishes, and that signals a minimum, a maximum or a saddle. In a space with infinitely many directions saddles are not the exception, and an oscillator travelling for longer than half a period supplies a stationary path with neighbours of strictly smaller action.

The real explanation is not available yet, and naming it stops anybody filling the gap with a story about nature being economical. In the last part of this book a quantum particle contributes from every route it might take, weighted by a phase built from that same number. Where the number changes at first order the neighbouring contributions point in all directions and cancel; where it does not, a whole neighbourhood shares one phase and survives.

6 · Constraints become trivial — the payoff

So far the action principle has cost effort and returned Newton's laws, which we already had. This section is where it starts paying.

6.1 · Generalised coordinates

A generalised coordinate system is any set of nnn numbers q1,…,qnq^{1},\dots,q^{n}q1,…,qn that fixes the configuration of the system, where nnn is the number of independent ways the system can move. The qqq's need not be lengths. They can be angles, areas, arc lengths along a wire, the amplitude of a normal mode, or anything else, and they need not have the same dimensions as each other.

Why this is allowed is the whole point of §3: the derivation of (1.2.23) never assumed anything about what the qiq^{i}qi meant. It assumed only that they could be varied independently. So the recipe is:

  1. Choose coordinates that automatically satisfy the constraints — one coordinate per genuine degree of freedom, so that every value of the qiq^{i}qi describes an allowed configuration and every allowed configuration corresponds to some qiq^{i}qi.
  2. Write TTT and VVV in terms of them.
  3. Turn the crank (1.2.23).

Constraint forces never appear, because in step 1 the constraint stopped being a force and became a coordinate.

6.2 · The pendulum, in three lines

A bob of mass mmm on a rigid massless rod of length ℓ\ellℓ, swinging in a vertical plane about a fixed pivot. Two Cartesian coordinates, one rigid constraint, so n=1n=1n=1; take θ\thetaθ, the angle from the downward vertical.

The bob moves on a circle of radius ℓ\ellℓ, so its speed is ℓθ˙\ell\dot\thetaℓθ˙ and its height relative to the pivot is −ℓcos⁡θ-\ell\cos\theta−ℓcosθ. Hence

T=12mℓ2θ˙2,V=−mgℓcos⁡θ,L=12mℓ2θ˙2+mgℓcos⁡θ. T = \half m\ell^{2}\dot\theta^{2}, \qquad V = -mg\ell\cos\theta, \qquad L = \half m\ell^{2}\dot\theta^{2} + mg\ell\cos\theta. T=21​mℓ2θ˙2,V=−mgℓcosθ,L=21​mℓ2θ˙2+mgℓcosθ. (1.2.36)

Two derivatives:

∂L∂θ˙=mℓ2θ˙,∂L∂θ=−mgℓsin⁡θ. \pdv{L}{\dot\theta} = m\ell^{2}\dot\theta, \qquad\qquad \pdv{L}{\theta} = -mg\ell\sin\theta. ∂θ˙∂L​=mℓ2θ˙,∂θ∂L​=−mgℓsinθ. (1.2.37)

Feed them to (1.2.22):

ddt(mℓ2θ˙)+mgℓsin⁡θ=0⟺θ¨=−gℓsin⁡θ. \dv{}{t}\big(m\ell^{2}\dot\theta\big) + mg\ell\sin\theta = 0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \ddot\theta = -\frac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta. dtd​(mℓ2θ˙)+mgℓsinθ=0⟺θ¨=−ℓg​sinθ. (1.2.38)

That is the whole derivation. No forces were resolved, no free-body diagram was drawn, and — the point — the tension in the rod never appeared. Chapter 1.1 got the same equation by resolving forces along and perpendicular to the rod, which required introducing the unknown tension F\mathcal{F}F, writing two component equations, and eliminating F\mathcal{F}F between them. Worked Example 1 does that side by side so you can count the lines.

Why is the tension absent here? Because the rod's tension is always perpendicular to the bob's motion, so it does no work. Energies are what LLL is built from, and a force that does no work contributes no energy, so it cannot appear in LLL. Meanwhile the geometric job the tension was doing — keeping the bob at distance ℓ\ellℓ — has been absorbed into the choice of θ\thetaθ as the coordinate, since every value of θ\thetaθ automatically has the bob at radius ℓ\ellℓ. The constraint has been converted from a force into a coordinate, and that trade is the central practical advantage of the Lagrangian formulation.

6.3 · A harder one, to show the method scales

Now the double pendulum: a rod of length ℓ1\ell_{1}ℓ1​ from a fixed pivot to mass m1m_{1}m1​, and a second rod of length ℓ2\ell_{2}ℓ2​ from m1m_{1}m1​ to m2m_{2}m2​. Four Cartesian coordinates, two rigid constraints, so n=2n=2n=2; take θ1\theta_{1}θ1​ and θ2\theta_{2}θ2​, each measured from the downward vertical.

Positions, with yyy measured downward from the pivot:

x1=ℓ1sin⁡θ1,y1=ℓ1cos⁡θ1,x2=ℓ1sin⁡θ1+ℓ2sin⁡θ2,y2=ℓ1cos⁡θ1+ℓ2cos⁡θ2. \begin{aligned} x_{1} &= \ell_{1}\sin\theta_{1}, & y_{1} &= \ell_{1}\cos\theta_{1},\\ x_{2} &= \ell_{1}\sin\theta_{1} + \ell_{2}\sin\theta_{2}, & y_{2} &= \ell_{1}\cos\theta_{1} + \ell_{2}\cos\theta_{2}. \end{aligned} x1​x2​​=ℓ1​sinθ1​,=ℓ1​sinθ1​+ℓ2​sinθ2​,​y1​y2​​=ℓ1​cosθ1​,=ℓ1​cosθ1​+ℓ2​cosθ2​.​ (1.2.39)

Differentiate and square. For the second mass, x˙22+y˙22=ℓ12θ˙12+ℓ22θ˙22+2ℓ1ℓ2θ˙1θ˙2(cos⁡θ1cos⁡θ2+sin⁡θ1sin⁡θ2)\dot x_{2}^{2}+\dot y_{2}^{2} = \ell_{1}^{2}\dot\theta_{1}^{2} + \ell_{2}^{2}\dot\theta_{2}^{2} + 2\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\dot\theta_{1}\dot\theta_{2}\big(\cos\theta_{1}\cos\theta_{2} + \sin\theta_{1}\sin\theta_{2}\big)x˙22​+y˙​22​=ℓ12​θ˙12​+ℓ22​θ˙22​+2ℓ1​ℓ2​θ˙1​θ˙2​(cosθ1​cosθ2​+sinθ1​sinθ2​), and the bracket collapses by the angle-subtraction identity. Heights are −y-y−y, so

L  =  12(m1+m2)ℓ12θ˙12+12m2ℓ22θ˙22+m2ℓ1ℓ2θ˙1θ˙2cos⁡(θ1−θ2)+(m1+m2)gℓ1cos⁡θ1+m2gℓ2cos⁡θ2. \begin{aligned} L \;=\; &\half(m_{1}+m_{2})\ell_{1}^{2}\dot\theta_{1}^{2} + \half m_{2}\ell_{2}^{2}\dot\theta_{2}^{2} + m_{2}\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\dot\theta_{1}\dot\theta_{2}\cos(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2})\\[3pt] &+ (m_{1}+m_{2})g\ell_{1}\cos\theta_{1} + m_{2}g\ell_{2}\cos\theta_{2}. \end{aligned} L=​21​(m1​+m2​)ℓ12​θ˙12​+21​m2​ℓ22​θ˙22​+m2​ℓ1​ℓ2​θ˙1​θ˙2​cos(θ1​−θ2​)+(m1​+m2​)gℓ1​cosθ1​+m2​gℓ2​cosθ2​.​ (1.2.40)

Two lines, and the dynamics is completely specified: apply (1.2.23) twice and you have the equations of motion, coupling and all. The Newtonian route requires four unknown constraint-force components (two rods, each exerting a force with two components on each of its ends), four vector equations, and the elimination of all four unknowns. The Lagrangian route needed no unknowns at all, because the coordinates (θ1,θ2)(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})(θ1​,θ2​) already encode both rigid rods.

This is the scaling argument. Adding a third link adds one coordinate, one term to TTT, one term to VVV, and one Euler–Lagrange equation. In the force picture it adds two more unknown constraint forces to be eliminated. The Lagrangian method grows linearly in the number of degrees of freedom; the force method grows with the number of constraints, which is exactly the quantity you were hoping to make go away.

Grind box — the double pendulum's kinetic energy, every step

Differentiate (1.2.39):

x˙1=ℓ1θ˙1cos⁡θ1,y˙1=−ℓ1θ˙1sin⁡θ1,x˙2=ℓ1θ˙1cos⁡θ1+ℓ2θ˙2cos⁡θ2,y˙2=−ℓ1θ˙1sin⁡θ1−ℓ2θ˙2sin⁡θ2. \begin{aligned} \dot x_{1} &= \ell_{1}\dot\theta_{1}\cos\theta_{1}, & \dot y_{1} &= -\ell_{1}\dot\theta_{1}\sin\theta_{1},\\ \dot x_{2} &= \ell_{1}\dot\theta_{1}\cos\theta_{1}+\ell_{2}\dot\theta_{2}\cos\theta_{2}, & \dot y_{2} &= -\ell_{1}\dot\theta_{1}\sin\theta_{1}-\ell_{2}\dot\theta_{2}\sin\theta_{2}. \end{aligned} x˙1​x˙2​​=ℓ1​θ˙1​cosθ1​,=ℓ1​θ˙1​cosθ1​+ℓ2​θ˙2​cosθ2​,​y˙​1​y˙​2​​=−ℓ1​θ˙1​sinθ1​,=−ℓ1​θ˙1​sinθ1​−ℓ2​θ˙2​sinθ2​.​

The first mass is easy: x˙12+y˙12=ℓ12θ˙12(cos⁡2θ1+sin⁡2θ1)=ℓ12θ˙12\dot x_{1}^{2}+\dot y_{1}^{2} = \ell_{1}^{2}\dot\theta_{1}^{2} (\cos^{2}\theta_{1}+\sin^{2}\theta_{1}) = \ell_{1}^{2}\dot\theta_{1}^{2}x˙12​+y˙​12​=ℓ12​θ˙12​(cos2θ1​+sin2θ1​)=ℓ12​θ˙12​. For the second, square both and add:

x˙22=ℓ12θ˙12cos⁡2θ1+ℓ22θ˙22cos⁡2θ2+2ℓ1ℓ2θ˙1θ˙2cos⁡θ1cos⁡θ2,y˙22=ℓ12θ˙12sin⁡2θ1+ℓ22θ˙22sin⁡2θ2+2ℓ1ℓ2θ˙1θ˙2sin⁡θ1sin⁡θ2. \begin{aligned} \dot x_{2}^{2} &= \ell_{1}^{2}\dot\theta_{1}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta_{1} + \ell_{2}^{2}\dot\theta_{2}^{2}\cos^{2}\theta_{2} + 2\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\dot\theta_{1}\dot\theta_{2}\cos\theta_{1}\cos\theta_{2},\\ \dot y_{2}^{2} &= \ell_{1}^{2}\dot\theta_{1}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta_{1} + \ell_{2}^{2}\dot\theta_{2}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta_{2} + 2\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\dot\theta_{1}\dot\theta_{2}\sin\theta_{1}\sin\theta_{2}. \end{aligned} x˙22​y˙​22​​=ℓ12​θ˙12​cos2θ1​+ℓ22​θ˙22​cos2θ2​+2ℓ1​ℓ2​θ˙1​θ˙2​cosθ1​cosθ2​,=ℓ12​θ˙12​sin2θ1​+ℓ22​θ˙22​sin2θ2​+2ℓ1​ℓ2​θ˙1​θ˙2​sinθ1​sinθ2​.​

The Pythagorean identity collapses the first two columns, and the cross terms combine through cos⁡θ1cos⁡θ2+sin⁡θ1sin⁡θ2=cos⁡(θ1−θ2)\cos\theta_{1}\cos\theta_{2}+\sin\theta_{1}\sin\theta_{2} = \cos(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2})cosθ1​cosθ2​+sinθ1​sinθ2​=cos(θ1​−θ2​):

x˙22+y˙22=ℓ12θ˙12+ℓ22θ˙22+2ℓ1ℓ2θ˙1θ˙2cos⁡(θ1−θ2). \dot x_{2}^{2}+\dot y_{2}^{2} = \ell_{1}^{2}\dot\theta_{1}^{2}+\ell_{2}^{2}\dot\theta_{2}^{2}+2\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\dot\theta_{1}\dot\theta_{2}\cos(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}). x˙22​+y˙​22​=ℓ12​θ˙12​+ℓ22​θ˙22​+2ℓ1​ℓ2​θ˙1​θ˙2​cos(θ1​−θ2​).

Then T=12m1ℓ12θ˙12+12m2(x˙22+y˙22)T=\half m_{1}\ell_{1}^{2}\dot\theta_{1}^{2} + \half m_{2}\big(\dot x_{2}^{2}+\dot y_{2}^{2}\big)T=21​m1​ℓ12​θ˙12​+21​m2​(x˙22​+y˙​22​), which on collecting the θ˙12\dot\theta_{1}^{2}θ˙12​ terms gives (1.2.40). With yyy measured downward, the height of mass jjj above the pivot is −yj-y_{j}−yj​, so V=−m1gy1−m2gy2V = -m_{1}gy_{1}-m_{2}gy_{2}V=−m1​gy1​−m2​gy2​, giving the two potential terms with the signs shown.

A structural remark you will need in Chapter 1.3. The kinetic energy came out as a quadratic form in the generalised velocities, T=12∑ijMij(θ) θ˙iθ˙jT=\half\sum_{ij}M_{ij}(\theta)\,\dot\theta^{i}\dot\theta^{j}T=21​∑ij​Mij​(θ)θ˙iθ˙j with

M(θ)=((m1+m2)ℓ12m2ℓ1ℓ2cos⁡(θ1−θ2)m2ℓ1ℓ2cos⁡(θ1−θ2)m2ℓ22), M(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} (m_{1}+m_{2})\ell_{1}^{2} & m_{2}\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\cos(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2})\\ m_{2}\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\cos(\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}) & m_{2}\ell_{2}^{2}\end{pmatrix}, M(θ)=((m1​+m2​)ℓ12​m2​ℓ1​ℓ2​cos(θ1​−θ2​)​m2​ℓ1​ℓ2​cos(θ1​−θ2​)m2​ℓ22​​),

symmetric and positive definite — the "mass matrix". That is not an accident of this example. Whenever the coordinate change from Cartesians is time-independent, TTT is always a positive-definite quadratic form in q˙\dot qq˙​, because it is 12∑ma∣x˙a∣2\half\sum m_{a}\abs{\dot{\vv x}_{a}}^{2}21​∑ma​∣x˙a​∣2 pushed through a linear map (Chapter 0.5). Positive-definiteness is what makes p=∂L/∂q˙p=\partial L/\partial\dot qp=∂L/∂q˙​ invertible for q˙\dot qq˙​, which is precisely the condition Chapter 1.3 needs for the Legendre transform to exist. And a metric-like symmetric positive-definite matrix that depends on position is exactly the object Chapter 3.3 calls a metric — the kinetic energy is a metric on configuration space, and free motion is a geodesic in it.

6.4 · When you want the constraint force: Lagrange multipliers

Sometimes the constraint force is the answer you need — you are designing the rod and want to know whether it will snap. Eliminating it was convenient; now we want it back. Chapter 0.6 already built the tool.

There, the problem was to make f(x)f(\vv x)f(x) stationary subject to g(x)=0g(\vv x)=0g(x)=0, and the resolution was to make the unconstrained function f−λ(g−c)f - \lambda(g-c)f−λ(g−c) stationary in both x\vv xx and λ\lambdaλ, trading a restriction on the search space for one extra equation and one extra unknown. Do exactly the same thing here, with the search space now a space of paths.

Suppose we use redundant coordinates q1,…,qNq^{1},\dots,q^{N}q1,…,qN (NNN larger than the number of degrees of freedom) subject to a constraint g(q,t)=0g(q,t)=0g(q,t)=0 that must hold at every instant. Consider the modified action

S~[q,λ]  =  ∫t1t2[L(q,q˙,t)  +  λ(t) g(q,t)]dt, \tilde S[q,\lambda] \;=\; \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\Big[L(q,\dot q,t) \;+\; \lambda(t)\,g(q,t)\Big]\dd t, S~[q,λ]=∫t1​t2​​[L(q,q˙​,t)+λ(t)g(q,t)]dt, (1.2.41)

where λ(t)\lambda(t)λ(t) — note: a function of time, one multiplier per instant, because the constraint must hold at every instant — is now one more variable to be varied over. Varying with respect to λ\lambdaλ is easy: λ\lambdaλ appears without its derivative, so (1.2.22) with ∂L~/∂λ˙=0\partial\tilde L/\partial\dot\lambda=0∂L~/∂λ˙=0 gives ∂L~/∂λ=g(q,t)=0\partial\tilde L/\partial\lambda = g(q,t) = 0∂L~/∂λ=g(q,t)=0. The constraint has been recovered as an equation of motion. Varying with respect to qiq^{i}qi gives

ddt ⁣(∂L∂q˙i)−∂L∂qi  =  λ ∂g∂qi. \dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}}\right) - \pdv{L}{q^{i}} \;=\; \lambda\,\pdv{g}{q^{i}}. dtd​(∂q˙​i∂L​)−∂qi∂L​=λ∂qi∂g​. (1.2.42)

Compare with (1.2.23). The left-hand side is the free Euler–Lagrange expression, which in Cartesian coordinates is p˙i−Fi\dot p_{i}-F_{i}p˙​i​−Fi​; so the right-hand side is an extra force, and λ ∂g/∂qi\lambda\,\partial g/\partial q^{i}λ∂g/∂qi is precisely the force that enforces the constraint. Two features are worth naming:

  • The constraint force points along ∇g\nabla g∇g — perpendicular to the constraint surface, exactly as Chapter 0.6 showed the gradient is normal to a level set. That is the mathematical content of "the constraint force does no work": motion allowed by the constraint is tangent to the surface, and a force normal to it has zero dot product with the motion.
  • The multiplier is the magnitude of that force, up to the normalisation of ggg — which matches Chapter 0.6's finding, up to a sign convention worth stating rather than stumbling over: Chapter 0.6 wrote L=f−λ(g−c)\mathcal L = f-\lambda(g-c)L=f−λ(g−c) and this section writes L+λgL+\lambda gL+λg, so the two λ\lambdaλ's are negatives of one another. Either way the multiplier is the sensitivity of the optimum to relaxing the constraint. Relax a rod's length and the work you must do is set by its tension. Same λ\lambdaλ, same meaning.

Worked example 1 runs this on the pendulum and recovers the tension explicitly. The same trade — restrict the space, or enlarge it and add a multiplier — reappears in Chapter 3.6 (where the metric is varied subject to nothing, but the analogous structure produces constraint equations) and in Chapter 6.3, where the "constraint" being imposed by a multiplier is a gauge condition.

In plain terms 1.2.6

Constraints were the first of the four failures, and they stop being one the moment you may choose your own variables. A bob on a string has one way to move, so describe it by one number, the angle, and every value of that number already puts the bob at the right distance from the pivot. The constraint has not been solved or eliminated but converted into a coordinate, and nothing is left to enforce.

The tension, which cost a page of algebra in the force picture and was then discarded, never appears at all. The reason fits in a sentence: a force perpendicular to the motion does no work, the scalar is built out of energies, and a force doing no work has no energy to contribute. Adding a second link adds one coordinate and one equation, where the force method adds two more unknowns — so only one of them grows with the thing you hoped to be rid of.

When the constraint force is the answer you want, because you are designing the rod and want to know whether it snaps, it returns by the device the toolkit built for optimising under restriction. The multiplier was described there as a price, the sensitivity of the best available value to relaxing the restriction. Here the price is the tension in newtons, and the identification is exact rather than analogy.

7 · Form invariance — the property that survives to general relativity

Here is the structural property that makes the Lagrangian formulation not merely convenient but necessary for everything after Chapter 2.

Claim. Let qi=qi(Q1,…,Qn,t)q^{i}=q^{i}(Q^{1},\dots,Q^{n},t)qi=qi(Q1,…,Qn,t) be any invertible, smooth change of coordinates (possibly time-dependent), and define the Lagrangian in the new coordinates by substitution,

L~(Q,Q˙,t)  ≡  L(q(Q,t),  q˙(Q,Q˙,t),  t). \tilde L\big(Q,\dot Q,t\big) \;\equiv\; L\Big(q(Q,t),\;\dot q(Q,\dot Q,t),\;t\Big). L~(Q,Q˙​,t)≡L(q(Q,t),q˙​(Q,Q˙​,t),t). (1.2.43)

Then Qa(t)Q^{a}(t)Qa(t) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations of L~\tilde LL~ if and only if qi(t)q^{i}(t)qi(t) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations of LLL.

The one-line reason. SSS is a number attached to a path. Relabelling which numbers you use to name the points of the path cannot change that number — you fed in the same physical path and got the same integral. So the function Φ(ϵ)=S[path deformed by ϵ]\Phi(\epsilon)=S[\text{path deformed by }\epsilon]Φ(ϵ)=S[path deformed by ϵ] is identical in both descriptions, and so is the statement Φ′(0)=0\Phi'(0)=0Φ′(0)=0. Stationarity is a property of the path, not of the names.

That argument is correct and it is the reason. But it is worth also seeing the derivative-level version, because the two lemmas it uses recur constantly.

Lemma 1 (cancellation of the dots). Differentiating qi(Q(t),t)q^{i}(Q(t),t)qi(Q(t),t) along the path,

q˙i  =  ∑a∂qi∂Qa Q˙a  +  ∂qi∂t. \dot q^{i} \;=\; \sum_{a}\pdv{q^{i}}{Q^{a}}\,\dot Q^{a} \;+\; \pdv{q^{i}}{t}. q˙​i=a∑​∂Qa∂qi​Q˙​a+∂t∂qi​. (1.2.44)

The right-hand side is linear in Q˙a\dot Q^{a}Q˙​a with coefficients depending only on QQQ and ttt. Reading off the coefficient,

∂q˙i∂Q˙a  =  ∂qi∂Qa. \pdv{\dot q^{i}}{\dot Q^{a}} \;=\; \pdv{q^{i}}{Q^{a}}. ∂Q˙​a∂q˙​i​=∂Qa∂qi​. (1.2.45)

Lemma 2 (partial and total derivatives commute). Differentiate (1.2.44) with respect to QaQ^{a}Qa at fixed Q˙\dot QQ˙​; separately take the total time derivative of ∂qi/∂Qa\partial q^{i}/\partial Q^{a}∂qi/∂Qa using the chain rule. Both give the same thing:

∂q˙i∂Qa  =  ∑b∂2qi∂Qa∂QbQ˙b+∂2qi∂Qa∂t  =  ddt ⁣(∂qi∂Qa), \pdv{\dot q^{i}}{Q^{a}} \;=\; \sum_{b}\frac{\partial^{2}q^{i}}{\partial Q^{a}\partial Q^{b}}\dot Q^{b} + \frac{\partial^{2}q^{i}}{\partial Q^{a}\partial t} \;=\; \dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{q^{i}}{Q^{a}}\right), ∂Qa∂q˙​i​=b∑​∂Qa∂Qb∂2qi​Q˙​b+∂Qa∂t∂2qi​=dtd​(∂Qa∂qi​), (1.2.46)

where the middle step used the equality of mixed partials (Chapter 0.6). Now the computation. From (1.2.43) and the chain rule, using Lemma 1,

∂L~∂Q˙a  =  ∑i∂L∂q˙i ∂q˙i∂Q˙a  =  ∑i∂L∂q˙i ∂qi∂Qa, \pdv{\tilde L}{\dot Q^{a}} \;=\; \sum_{i}\pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}}\,\pdv{\dot q^{i}}{\dot Q^{a}} \;=\; \sum_{i}\pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}}\,\pdv{q^{i}}{Q^{a}}, ∂Q˙​a∂L~​=i∑​∂q˙​i∂L​∂Q˙​a∂q˙​i​=i∑​∂q˙​i∂L​∂Qa∂qi​, (1.2.47)

and, since L~\tilde LL~ depends on QaQ^{a}Qa both directly and through q˙\dot qq˙​,

∂L~∂Qa  =  ∑i[∂L∂qi ∂qi∂Qa+∂L∂q˙i ∂q˙i∂Qa]. \pdv{\tilde L}{Q^{a}} \;=\; \sum_{i}\left[\pdv{L}{q^{i}}\,\pdv{q^{i}}{Q^{a}} + \pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}}\,\pdv{\dot q^{i}}{Q^{a}}\right]. ∂Qa∂L~​=i∑​[∂qi∂L​∂Qa∂qi​+∂q˙​i∂L​∂Qa∂q˙​i​]. (1.2.48)

Take d/dt\dd/\dd td/dt of (1.2.47) with the product rule and subtract (1.2.48):

ddt∂L~∂Q˙a−∂L~∂Qa  =  ∑i{[ddt∂L∂q˙i]∂qi∂Qa+∂L∂q˙i ddt ⁣(∂qi∂Qa)−∂L∂qi∂qi∂Qa−∂L∂q˙i∂q˙i∂Qa}. \begin{aligned} \dv{}{t}\pdv{\tilde L}{\dot Q^{a}} - \pdv{\tilde L}{Q^{a}} \;=\; \sum_{i}\Bigg\{&\left[\dv{}{t}\pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}}\right]\pdv{q^{i}}{Q^{a}} + \pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}}\,\dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{q^{i}}{Q^{a}}\right)\\ &-\pdv{L}{q^{i}}\pdv{q^{i}}{Q^{a}} - \pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}}\pdv{\dot q^{i}}{Q^{a}}\Bigg\}. \end{aligned} dtd​∂Q˙​a∂L~​−∂Qa∂L~​=i∑​{​[dtd​∂q˙​i∂L​]∂Qa∂qi​+∂q˙​i∂L​dtd​(∂Qa∂qi​)−∂qi∂L​∂Qa∂qi​−∂q˙​i∂L​∂Qa∂q˙​i​}.​ (1.2.49)

By Lemma 2 the second and fourth terms are equal and cancel. What is left factorises:

  ddt∂L~∂Q˙a−∂L~∂Qa  =  ∑i[ddt∂L∂q˙i−∂L∂qi]∂qi∂Qa.   \boxed{\;\dv{}{t}\pdv{\tilde L}{\dot Q^{a}} - \pdv{\tilde L}{Q^{a}} \;=\; \sum_{i}\left[\dv{}{t}\pdv{L}{\dot q^{i}} - \pdv{L}{q^{i}}\right]\pdv{q^{i}}{Q^{a}}.\;} dtd​∂Q˙​a∂L~​−∂Qa∂L~​=i∑​[dtd​∂q˙​i∂L​−∂qi∂L​]∂Qa∂qi​.​ (1.2.50)

The Euler–Lagrange expressions transform into each other by multiplication by the Jacobian matrix ∂qi/∂Qa\partial q^{i}/\partial Q^{a}∂qi/∂Qa, which is invertible because the coordinate change is. So one set vanishes exactly when the other does. ■\blacksquare■

7.1 · Why this matters more than it looks

Now the contrast. F=maF=maF=ma is not form invariant. Write Newton's law in plane polar coordinates and it does not read mr¨=Frm\ddot r = F_{r}mr¨=Fr​. The acceleration of a particle in polar coordinates has extra pieces:

a  =  (r¨−rθ˙2) r^  +  (rθ¨+2r˙θ˙) θ^. \vv a \;=\; \big(\ddot r - r\dot\theta^{2}\big)\,\hat{\vv r} \;+\; \big(r\ddot\theta + 2\dot r\dot\theta\big)\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}. a=(r¨−rθ˙2)r^+(rθ¨+2r˙θ˙)θ^. (1.2.51)

The −rθ˙2-r\dot\theta^{2}−rθ˙2 is the centrifugal term and the 2r˙θ˙2\dot r\dot\theta2r˙θ˙ is the Coriolis term, and they arise because the basis vectors r^,θ^\hat{\vv r},\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}r^,θ^ themselves rotate as the particle moves, so differentiating a vector twice requires differentiating the basis too. Getting (1.2.51) honestly takes half a page of unit-vector derivatives.

Now get it from the Lagrangian. In polar coordinates T=12m(r˙2+r2θ˙2)T=\half m(\dot r^{2}+r^{2}\dot\theta^{2})T=21​m(r˙2+r2θ˙2) — just Pythagoras on the radial and tangential velocity components — so with a potential V(r,θ)V(r,\theta)V(r,θ),

L=12m(r˙2+r2θ˙2)−V(r,θ). L = \half m\big(\dot r^{2}+r^{2}\dot\theta^{2}\big) - V(r,\theta). L=21​m(r˙2+r2θ˙2)−V(r,θ). (1.2.52)

Turn the crank. For q=rq=rq=r: ∂L/∂r˙=mr˙\partial L/\partial\dot r = m\dot r∂L/∂r˙=mr˙ and ∂L/∂r=mrθ˙2−∂V/∂r\partial L/\partial r = mr\dot\theta^{2} - \partial V/\partial r∂L/∂r=mrθ˙2−∂V/∂r, so

mr¨−mrθ˙2=−∂V∂r. m\ddot r - mr\dot\theta^{2} = -\pdv{V}{r}. mr¨−mrθ˙2=−∂r∂V​. (1.2.53)

For q=θq=\thetaq=θ: ∂L/∂θ˙=mr2θ˙\partial L/\partial\dot\theta = mr^{2}\dot\theta∂L/∂θ˙=mr2θ˙ and ∂L/∂θ=−∂V/∂θ\partial L/\partial\theta = -\partial V/\partial\theta∂L/∂θ=−∂V/∂θ, so

ddt(mr2θ˙)=−∂V∂θ⟺m(rθ¨+2r˙θ˙)=−1r∂V∂θ. \dv{}{t}\big(mr^{2}\dot\theta\big) = -\pdv{V}{\theta} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad m\big(r\ddot\theta + 2\dot r\dot\theta\big) = -\frac{1}{r}\pdv{V}{\theta}. dtd​(mr2θ˙)=−∂θ∂V​⟺m(rθ¨+2r˙θ˙)=−r1​∂θ∂V​. (1.2.54)

Both centrifugal and Coriolis terms appeared automatically, from differentiating a scalar. No unit vectors were differentiated; no fictitious forces had to be remembered. And (1.2.54) hands you a bonus: if VVV does not depend on θ\thetaθ, the left side says mr2θ˙mr^{2}\dot\thetamr2θ˙ is constant. Angular momentum conservation, for free, because θ\thetaθ was missing from LLL.

Why this decides the shape of the rest of the book

Newton's second law is a relation between vector components, and vector components transform in a complicated way when the basis varies from point to point. The law therefore has a privileged coordinate system — Cartesian — in which it is simple, and grows correction terms everywhere else.

General relativity has no global Cartesian coordinates. Not "it's awkward to find them"; there provably are none, because spacetime is curved, and Chapter 3.4 will make that a precise statement about a tensor that cannot be made to vanish. A formulation of physics that is simple only in a coordinate system that does not exist is not a formulation of physics. It is a special case.

The action is a scalar: a single number per path, with no components to transform. (1.2.50) says its stationarity condition therefore keeps the same shape in every coordinate system. That is why Chapters 2.6, 3.6, 5.2 and 6.4 all consist of the same sentence — "write down the most general scalar action invariant under the symmetry you believe in, and vary it" — and why they never once resolve a force.

Familiar ground

You already run a variational principle. When you fit a model by maximum likelihood you do not write down an estimator. You write down a scalar functional of the parameters, the log-likelihood ℓ(θ)\ell(\theta)ℓ(θ), declare that the answer is where it is stationary, and let the stationarity condition

∂ℓ∂θ  =  0 \pdv{\ell}{\theta} \;=\; 0 ∂θ∂ℓ​=0

— the score equation — produce the estimator. For a normal mean it produces the sample mean; for a Cox model it produces something you would never have guessed. Chapter 0.6 used the second derivative of that same surface: the Hessian at the peak is the observed information, and its inverse is the covariance matrix of the estimate. Here we are using the first derivative instead, and the parallel is exact: specify a scalar to be made stationary, and the equations you actually wanted are its stationarity condition. The Euler–Lagrange equation is the score equation of physics. The Hessian's role — telling you whether the stationary point is a maximum, a minimum, or neither — is played here by the second variation, which is exactly what the harmonic-oscillator warning callout computed.

The correspondence goes further than an analogy, into literally the same mathematics, the moment your unknown is a function rather than a parameter vector. Fit a smooth dose–response curve by penalised least squares: over all functions fff, minimise

J[f]  =  ∑j(yj−f(xj))2  +  λ∫abf′′(x)2 dx. J[f] \;=\; \sum_{j}\big(y_{j}-f(x_{j})\big)^{2} \;+\; \lambda\int_{a}^{b} f''(x)^{2}\,\dd x. J[f]=j∑​(yj​−f(xj​))2+λ∫ab​f′′(x)2dx.

That is a functional on an infinite-dimensional space, and finding its minimiser is the calculus of variations, not statistics. Vary f→f+ϵηf\to f+\epsilon\etaf→f+ϵη; the penalty term contributes 2λ∫f′′η′′ dx2\lambda\int f''\eta''\,\dd x2λ∫f′′η′′dx, and integrating by parts twice — the same move as §3.3, performed once more — turns ∫f′′η′′\int f''\eta''∫f′′η′′ into ∫f′′′′η\int f''''\eta∫f′′′′η plus boundary terms. Between data points, where the first sum contributes nothing, the Euler–Lagrange equation is therefore the one derived in §3.5's grind box with F=λf′′2F=\lambda f''^{2}F=λf′′2, namely

f′′′′(x)=0, f''''(x) = 0, f′′′′(x)=0,

whose solutions are exactly the cubic polynomials. That is why the answer is a cubic spline — not because someone chose cubics, but because they are the kernel of the Euler–Lagrange operator of the roughness penalty. And the boundary terms that by-parts leaves behind, having no fixed-endpoint condition to kill them, must vanish on their own: f′′=f′′′=0f''=f'''=0f′′=f′′′=0 at the outer knots, which forces the fitted curve to be linear beyond them. If you have ever wondered why a restricted cubic spline is constrained to be linear in the tails, that is the answer, and it is a boundary term in a calculus-of-variations problem. Same manoeuvre, same integration by parts, same vanishing boundary term as §3.3 — only the interpretation differs.

In plain terms 1.2.7

A number attached to a path has no components, and having no components is the whole of why it survives. Relabelling which numbers you use to name the points of a path cannot change the number the path was assigned, so the statement that this number stops changing is a fact about the path rather than about the naming. The equations following from it therefore keep their shape under any smooth invertible change of coordinates, including ones nobody has tabulated.

Set that beside the polar-coordinate embarrassment of the previous chapter. The centrifugal and Coriolis terms, which took half a page of differentiating rotating basis directions to produce, now drop out of differentiating a scalar, with no unit vectors touched and no fictitious force to be remembered. The same calculation hands over a conservation law for nothing, since the angle is absent from the scalar and an absent coordinate has a conjugate momentum that cannot move.

This is a property deciding the remainder of the book rather than a convenience. A curved spacetime provably admits no global straight grid, so a formulation simple only in such a grid is unusable there, while a formulation whose entire input is one number per path does not notice. Everything from here to the last chapter consists of choosing a scalar and making it stationary, and this is the reason it can.

8 · One equation to rule them all — a preview

Everything so far has a path x(t)x(t)x(t): one independent variable, ttt, and finitely many dependent ones. Physics after Chapter 5 has fields: a quantity ϕ\phiϕ defined at every point of spacetime, so that the dependent variable is indexed by four independent ones, xμ=(t,x,y,z)x^{\mu}=(t,x,y,z)xμ=(t,x,y,z).

The generalisation writes itself. Replace the Lagrangian by a Lagrangian density L(ϕ,∂μϕ)\mathcal{L}\big(\phi,\partial_{\mu}\phi\big)L(ϕ,∂μ​ϕ) and the time integral by an integral over a region Ω\OmegaΩ of spacetime:

S[ϕ]  =  ∫ΩL(ϕ,∂μϕ) d4x. S[\phi] \;=\; \int_{\Omega}\mathcal{L}\big(\phi,\partial_{\mu}\phi\big)\,\dd^{4}x. S[ϕ]=∫Ω​L(ϕ,∂μ​ϕ)d4x. (1.2.55)

Now repeat §3 verbatim. Vary ϕ→ϕ+ϵη\phi\to\phi+\epsilon\etaϕ→ϕ+ϵη with η\etaη vanishing on the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega∂Ω instead of at two endpoints. Differentiate under the integral sign. Linearise the integrand by the chain rule:

δS  =  ∫Ω[∂L∂ϕ η  +  ∂L∂(∂μϕ) ∂μη]d4x. \delta S \;=\; \int_{\Omega}\left[\pdv{\mathcal{L}}{\phi}\,\eta \;+\; \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}\phi)}\,\partial_{\mu}\eta\right]\dd^{4}x. δS=∫Ω​[∂ϕ∂L​η+∂(∂μ​ϕ)∂L​∂μ​η]d4x. (1.2.56)

Integrate by parts to move the derivative off ∂μη\partial_{\mu}\eta∂μ​η — in four dimensions "by parts" means the divergence theorem of Chapter 0.7, which converts ∫Ω∂μ(⋯ )μd4x\int_{\Omega}\partial_{\mu}(\cdots)^{\mu}\dd^{4}x∫Ω​∂μ​(⋯)μd4x into a surface integral over ∂Ω\partial\Omega∂Ω. That surface term dies because η\etaη vanishes there — same reason, same sentence. Apply the fundamental lemma, whose proof needs only the obvious four-dimensional bump function. Out comes

  ∂μ ⁣(∂L∂(∂μϕ))  −  ∂L∂ϕ  =  0.   \boxed{\;\partial_{\mu}\!\left(\pdv{\mathcal{L}}{(\partial_{\mu}\phi)}\right) \;-\; \pdv{\mathcal{L}}{\phi} \;=\; 0.\;} ∂μ​(∂(∂μ​ϕ)∂L​)−∂ϕ∂L​=0.​ (1.2.57)

Put (1.2.57) beside (1.2.22). The dictionary is t→xμt\to x^{\mu}t→xμ, dt→d4x\dd t\to\dd^{4}xdt→d4x, ddt→∂μ\dv{}{t}\to\partial_{\mu}dtd​→∂μ​, x˙→∂μϕ\dot x\to\partial_{\mu}\phix˙→∂μ​ϕ, and nothing else. The derivation you did in §3 is the derivation that produces every field equation in physics. Chapter 5.2 develops this properly, including what happens when ϕ\phiϕ carries indices and what Lorentz invariance demands of L\mathcal{L}L; there is no point duplicating it here. The point is that there is nothing new to learn — only the same four moves in more dimensions.
