The overall sign of the gravitational entry depends on the metric signature, and with this book's (+,−,−,−)(+,-,-,-)(+,−,−,−) it is negative. Chapter 3.6 derives it rather than adopting it, and says in place why texts using the opposite signature write it the other way round.

Eight lines. Between them they contain classical mechanics, special relativity, electromagnetism, gravitation, quantum field theory, the strong and electroweak interactions, and string theory. Every one is fed to (1.2.22) or (1.2.57), and the output is the equations of motion of that theory. The rest of this book is, to a first approximation, the story of how each of those eight lines gets chosen — which is always the same story: pick a symmetry, and write the most general scalar invariant under it.

In plain terms 1.2.8

Replace the single independent variable by the four of spacetime, let the quantity being varied be defined at every point rather than at every instant, and the four moves run again word for word. The nudge must now vanish on the boundary of a region instead of at two endpoints, the by-parts step becomes the divergence theorem, and the term it leaves behind dies for the same reason as before. Out comes one equation, and it is every field equation in physics.

The chapter closes with eight lines of scalar, one per theory: a free particle, a relativistic one, the electromagnetic field, gravity, a scalar field, the electron, the strong and weak interactions, and a string. Between them they hold nearly everything the rest of this book is about, each is fed to the same machine, and what comes back is the equations of motion of that subject. Not analogues of them, but them.

What has been bought is worth stating flatly. The input to physics is no longer a list of forces to be discovered one at a time but a single number attached to each history, and the output follows from one condition imposed on it. What has not been bought is any reason to prefer one such number to another, which is the whole of what remains, and two chapters from now a symmetry supplies it.

9 · Worked examples

Worked example 1 — the pendulum, three ways, with the tension recovered

(a) The Newtonian route, as in Chapter 1.1. The bob has two forces on it: gravity mgm\vv gmg downward, and the rod tension F\mathcal{F}F directed along the rod toward the pivot. Resolve along the two natural directions. Tangentially (in the direction of increasing θ\thetaθ), gravity contributes −mgsin⁡θ-mg\sin\theta−mgsinθ and the tension contributes nothing, while the tangential acceleration is ℓθ¨\ell\ddot\thetaℓθ¨:

mℓθ¨=−mgsin⁡θ. m\ell\ddot\theta = -mg\sin\theta. mℓθ¨=−mgsinθ.

Radially (toward the pivot), the acceleration is the centripetal ℓθ˙2\ell\dot\theta^{2}ℓθ˙2, and the inward forces are F\mathcal{F}F minus the inward component of gravity mgcos⁡θmg\cos\thetamgcosθ:

mℓθ˙2=F−mgcos⁡θ. m\ell\dot\theta^{2} = \mathcal{F} - mg\cos\theta. mℓθ˙2=F−mgcosθ.

Two equations, two unknowns (θ,F)(\theta,\mathcal{F})(θ,F). The first is what we wanted; the second exists only to determine F\mathcal{F}F, which we then discard. To write either of them you had to know in advance that the acceleration in polar coordinates has a centripetal piece — that is, you had to have (1.2.51) already.

(b) The Lagrangian route. One coordinate, θ\thetaθ. Kinetic energy 12mℓ2θ˙2\half m\ell^{2}\dot\theta^{2}21​mℓ2θ˙2, potential −mgℓcos⁡θ-mg\ell\cos\theta−mgℓcosθ,

L=12mℓ2θ˙2+mgℓcos⁡θ⟹ddt(mℓ2θ˙)+mgℓsin⁡θ=0⟹θ¨=−gℓsin⁡θ. \begin{aligned} L &= \half m\ell^{2}\dot\theta^{2} + mg\ell\cos\theta\\[3pt] &\Longrightarrow\quad \dv{}{t}\big(m\ell^{2}\dot\theta\big) + mg\ell\sin\theta = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ddot\theta = -\frac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta. \end{aligned} L​=21​mℓ2θ˙2+mgℓcosθ⟹dtd​(mℓ2θ˙)+mgℓsinθ=0⟹θ¨=−ℓg​sinθ.​

One unknown, one equation, no tension, no unit-vector derivatives, no (1.2.51). The count is: (a) needed two vector resolutions and one elimination; (b) needed two partial derivatives.

(c) Recovering the tension with a multiplier. Now deliberately do not impose the constraint. Use polar coordinates (r,θ)(r,\theta)(r,θ) in the plane, so that

L=12m(r˙2+r2θ˙2)+mgrcos⁡θ, L = \half m\big(\dot r^{2}+r^{2}\dot\theta^{2}\big) + mgr\cos\theta, L=21​m(r˙2+r2θ˙2)+mgrcosθ,

with the constraint g(r)=r−ℓ=0g(r) = r-\ell = 0g(r)=r−ℓ=0. Following (1.2.41), vary L~=L+λ(t) (r−ℓ)\tilde L = L + \lambda(t)\,(r-\ell)L~=L+λ(t)(r−ℓ). The λ\lambdaλ equation returns r=ℓr=\ellr=ℓ. The θ\thetaθ equation, with rrr then set to ℓ\ellℓ, returns the pendulum equation again. The rrr equation is the new information:

ddt(mr˙)−(mrθ˙2+mgcos⁡θ+λ)=0. \dv{}{t}\big(m\dot r\big) - \Big(mr\dot\theta^{2} + mg\cos\theta + \lambda\Big) = 0. dtd​(mr˙)−(mrθ˙2+mgcosθ+λ)=0.

On the constraint surface r≡ℓr\equiv\ellr≡ℓ, so r˙=r¨=0\dot r=\ddot r=0r˙=r¨=0, and

λ=−m(ℓθ˙2+gcos⁡θ). \lambda = -m\big(\ell\dot\theta^{2} + g\cos\theta\big). λ=−m(ℓθ˙2+gcosθ).

The generalised constraint force is λ ∂g/∂r=λ\lambda\,\partial g/\partial r = \lambdaλ∂g/∂r=λ, and it is negative — directed toward decreasing rrr, i.e. toward the pivot, which is exactly the direction a rod pulls. Its magnitude is

F=∣λ∣=m(ℓθ˙2+gcos⁡θ), \mathcal{F} = \abs{\lambda} = m\big(\ell\dot\theta^{2}+g\cos\theta\big), F=∣λ∣=m(ℓθ˙2+gcosθ),

identical to what route (a) produced. The multiplier is the tension. Note the two contributions, both physically sensible: mgcos⁡θmg\cos\thetamgcosθ holds up the component of weight along the rod, and mℓθ˙2m\ell\dot\theta^{2}mℓθ˙2 supplies the centripetal force. At the bottom of a swing released from horizontal, energy conservation gives ℓθ˙2=2g\ell\dot\theta^{2}=2gℓθ˙2=2g so F=3mg\mathcal{F}=3mgF=3mg — the standard result, obtained here without ever drawing a free-body diagram.

Small oscillations, since we are here. For ∣θ∣≪1\abs{\theta}\ll1∣θ∣≪1, sin⁡θ≈θ\sin\theta\approx\thetasinθ≈θ (Chapter 0.3) and (1.2.38) becomes θ¨=−(g/ℓ)θ\ddot\theta = -(g/\ell)\thetaθ¨=−(g/ℓ)θ: the harmonic oscillator of Chapter 0.8, with ω=g/ℓ\omega=\sqrt{g/\ell}ω=g/ℓ​ and period 2πℓ/g2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}2πℓ/g​ — the formula Chapter 0.1 differentiated logarithmically in its first worked example, now derived rather than quoted.

Worked example 2 — geodesics: the straight line, and the great circle

Strip away the physics. Take the arc-length functional (1.2.1) and ask which curve makes it stationary. This is the purest possible variational problem — no masses, no forces, no time — and it is the one that becomes gravity.

(a) In the plane. Minimise A[y]=∫ab1+y′2 dx\mathcal{A}[y]=\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+y'^{2}}\,\dd xA[y]=∫ab​1+y′2​dx between fixed endpoints. Here xxx plays the role of ttt and yyy the role of the coordinate, so the Euler–Lagrange equation (1.2.22) applies with F(y,y′)=1+y′2F(y,y')=\sqrt{1+y'^{2}}F(y,y′)=1+y′2​. Since FFF does not contain yyy at all,

∂F∂y=0⟹ddx ⁣(∂F∂y′)=0⟹∂F∂y′=y′1+y′2=c \pdv{F}{y} = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dv{}{x}\!\left(\pdv{F}{y'}\right) = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \pdv{F}{y'} = \frac{y'}{\sqrt{1+y'^{2}}} = c ∂y∂F​=0⟹dxd​(∂y′∂F​)=0⟹∂y′∂F​=1+y′2​y′​=c

for some constant ccc. Do not stop there — the equation still has to be solved for y′y'y′. Square both sides and clear the denominator:

y′2=c2(1+y′2)⟹y′2(1−c2)=c2⟹y′=c1−c2  ≡  m, y'^{2} = c^{2}\big(1+y'^{2}\big) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y'^{2}\big(1-c^{2}\big) = c^{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y' = \frac{c}{\sqrt{1-c^{2}}} \;\equiv\; m, y′2=c2(1+y′2)⟹y′2(1−c2)=c2⟹y′=1−c2​c​≡m,

a constant. (The division is legitimate: ∣c∣=∣y′∣/1+y′2<1\abs{c}=\abs{y'}/\sqrt{1+y'^{2}} \lt 1∣c∣=∣y′∣/1+y′2​<1 for every real y′y'y′, so 1−c2>01-c^{2} \gt 01−c2>0 always.) Integrating, y=mx+by = mx + by=mx+b. The straight line, from a variational principle — and note that we never assumed the answer was a line, or that it was smooth beyond C1C^{1}C1, or anything else. We asked for stationarity and got straightness.

(b) On a sphere. Now do the identical calculation with a different notion of distance. On the unit sphere with polar angle θ\thetaθ (from the north pole) and azimuth ϕ\phiϕ, an infinitesimal displacement has length

ds2=dθ2+sin⁡2θ dϕ2, \dd s^{2} = \dd\theta^{2} + \sin^{2}\theta\,\dd\phi^{2}, ds2=dθ2+sin2θdϕ2,

because moving in θ\thetaθ traverses a great circle of radius 111 while moving in ϕ\phiϕ traverses a circle of latitude of radius sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ. Parametrising the curve as ϕ(θ)\phi(\theta)ϕ(θ),

A[ϕ]=∫θ1θ21+sin⁡2θ  ϕ′2  dθ,F(θ,ϕ′)=1+sin⁡2θ ϕ′2. \mathcal{A}[\phi] = \int_{\theta_{1}}^{\theta_{2}}\sqrt{1+\sin^{2}\theta\;\phi'^{2}}\;\dd\theta, \qquad F(\theta,\phi') = \sqrt{1+\sin^{2}\theta\,\phi'^{2}}. A[ϕ]=∫θ1​θ2​​1+sin2θϕ′2​dθ,F(θ,ϕ′)=1+sin2θϕ′2​.

Again FFF contains no ϕ\phiϕ, so again ∂F/∂ϕ′\partial F/\partial\phi'∂F/∂ϕ′ is constant:

sin⁡2θ  ϕ′1+sin⁡2θ ϕ′2  =  k. \frac{\sin^{2}\theta\;\phi'}{\sqrt{1+\sin^{2}\theta\,\phi'^{2}}} \;=\; k. 1+sin2θϕ′2​sin2θϕ′​=k.

Take the case k=0k=0k=0 first. Since sin⁡θ≠0\sin\theta\neq0sinθ=0 away from the poles, k=0k=0k=0 forces ϕ′=0\phi'=0ϕ′=0, so ϕ=\phi=ϕ= constant: the curve is a meridian, which is a great circle.

That single case is enough, because of a symmetry we can check directly. The metric dθ2+sin⁡2θ dϕ2\dd\theta^{2}+\sin^{2}\theta\,\dd\phi^{2}dθ2+sin2θdϕ2 is the ordinary Euclidean length restricted to the sphere ∣r∣=1\abs{\vv r}=1∣r∣=1, and rotations of R3\R^{3}R3 preserve Euclidean length and map the sphere to itself — so a rotation carries curves to curves of the same length, and therefore carries stationary curves to stationary curves. Given any two points on the sphere, rotate so that both lie on a common meridian. The stationary curve joining them is then a meridian arc; rotating back, the stationary curve joining the original two points is the image of a meridian, which is a great circle. ■\blacksquare■ (The general k≠0k\neq0k=0 case can also be integrated directly, and gives the same answer; see the grind box.)

What just happened. The same functional, ∫ds\int\dd s∫ds, gave a straight line in one geometry and a great circle in another. The only input that changed was the formula for ds\dd sds — the metric. The variational principle did not change at all.

Chapter 3.3 will write ds2=gμν dxμdxν\dd s^{2}=g_{\mu\nu}\,\dd x^{\mu}\dd x^{\nu}ds2=gμν​dxμdxν for a metric on curved spacetime, feed ∫ds\int\dd s∫ds into exactly this machinery, and call the resulting Euler–Lagrange equation the geodesic equation. A planet orbiting the sun will turn out to be doing what the great circle does — travelling as straight as the geometry permits. Gravity will not be a force in that description; it will be the metric. Nothing about the method in this worked example will change. Only ds\dd sds.

Grind box — integrating the sphere's geodesic equation in the general case

Solve sin⁡2θ ϕ′/1+sin⁡2θ ϕ′2=k\sin^{2}\theta\,\phi'/\sqrt{1+\sin^{2}\theta\,\phi'^{2}} = ksin2θϕ′/1+sin2θϕ′2​=k for ϕ′\phi'ϕ′. Square and cross-multiply:

sin⁡4θ ϕ′2=k2(1+sin⁡2θ ϕ′2)  ⟹  ϕ′2sin⁡2θ(sin⁡2θ−k2)=k2  ⟹  ϕ′=ksin⁡θsin⁡2θ−k2. \sin^{4}\theta\,\phi'^{2} = k^{2}\big(1+\sin^{2}\theta\,\phi'^{2}\big) \;\Longrightarrow\; \phi'^{2}\sin^{2}\theta\big(\sin^{2}\theta-k^{2}\big) = k^{2} \;\Longrightarrow\; \phi' = \frac{k}{\sin\theta\sqrt{\sin^{2}\theta-k^{2}}}. sin4θϕ′2=k2(1+sin2θϕ′2)⟹ϕ′2sin2θ(sin2θ−k2)=k2⟹ϕ′=sinθsin2θ−k2​k​.

ϕ−ϕ0=∫k dθsin⁡2θ1−k2−k2u2=−∫k du1−k2−k2u2=−∫duA2−u2,A2≡1−k2k2. \phi-\phi_{0} = \int\frac{k\,\dd\theta}{\sin^{2}\theta\sqrt{1-k^{2}-k^{2}u^{2}}} = -\int\frac{k\,\dd u}{\sqrt{1-k^{2}-k^{2}u^{2}}} = -\int\frac{\dd u}{\sqrt{A^{2}-u^{2}}}, \quad A^{2}\equiv\frac{1-k^{2}}{k^{2}}. ϕ−ϕ0​=∫sin2θ1−k2−k2u2​kdθ​=−∫1−k2−k2u2​kdu​=−∫A2−u2​du​,A2≡k21−k2​.

Hence ϕ−ϕ0=−arcsin⁡(u/A)\phi-\phi_{0} = -\arcsin(u/A)ϕ−ϕ0​=−arcsin(u/A), i.e. cot⁡θ=−Asin⁡(ϕ−ϕ0)\cot\theta = -A\sin(\phi-\phi_{0})cotθ=−Asin(ϕ−ϕ0​). Multiply through by sin⁡θ\sin\thetasinθ and expand the sine:

cos⁡θ=−Asin⁡θ(sin⁡ϕcos⁡ϕ0−cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕ0). \cos\theta = -A\sin\theta\big(\sin\phi\cos\phi_{0}-\cos\phi\sin\phi_{0}\big). cosθ=−Asinθ(sinϕcosϕ0​−cosϕsinϕ0​).

Now recognise the Cartesian coordinates of a point on the unit sphere: X=sin⁡θcos⁡ϕX=\sin\theta\cos\phiX=sinθcosϕ, Y=sin⁡θsin⁡ϕY=\sin\theta\sin\phiY=sinθsinϕ, Z=cos⁡θZ=\cos\thetaZ=cosθ. The equation becomes

(Asin⁡ϕ0)X  −  (Acos⁡ϕ0)Y  −  Z  =  0, \big(A\sin\phi_{0}\big)X \;-\; \big(A\cos\phi_{0}\big)Y \;-\; Z \;=\; 0, (Asinϕ0​)X−(Acosϕ0​)Y−Z=0,

which is a plane through the origin. A plane through the centre of a sphere cuts it in a great circle. So every solution, for every kkk, is a great circle — the k=0k=0k=0 case being the limit in which the plane contains the polar axis. (Verified numerically to 7×10−167\times10^{-16}7×10−16 for A=0.8A=0.8A=0.8, ϕ0=0.4\phi_{0}=0.4ϕ0​=0.4.)

Notice that k=∂F/∂ϕ′k=\partial F/\partial\phi'k=∂F/∂ϕ′ is conserved because ϕ\phiϕ is absent from FFF — the same structure that gave angular momentum conservation in (1.2.54). On a sphere it is the statement that a geodesic's bearing satisfies sin⁡θcos⁡(bearing)=\sin\theta\cos(\text{bearing})=sinθcos(bearing)= constant, which navigators call Clairaut's relation and which is the reason a great-circle route from London to Tokyo goes over the Arctic. It is Noether's theorem (Chapter 1.4), arriving three chapters early disguised as cartography.

10 · Your turn

Problem 1 — the brachistochrone

A bead slides without friction down a wire from the origin to a lower point, starting from rest, under gravity ggg. Let yyy be measured downward. Set up the travel-time functional, reduce it with the fact that the integrand has no explicit xxx-dependence, and integrate the resulting equation to find the curve. (This is the problem Johann Bernoulli posed to Europe in 1696; Newton is said to have solved it overnight and returned it anonymously, whereupon Bernoulli reportedly recognised the author "as the lion by his claw".)

Solution

Set-up. Energy conservation from rest gives 12mv2=mgy\half mv^{2}=mgy21​mv2=mgy, so v=2gyv=\sqrt{2gy}v=2gy​ — independent of the shape of the wire, which is what makes the problem tractable. The time to traverse an element of arc is ds/v\dd s/vds/v, so

T[y]=∫0x11+y′22gy  dx  ≡  ∫0x1F(y,y′) dx. \mathcal{T}[y] = \int_{0}^{x_{1}}\frac{\sqrt{1+y'^{2}}}{\sqrt{2gy}}\;\dd x \;\equiv\; \int_{0}^{x_{1}} F(y,y')\,\dd x. T[y]=∫0x1​​2gy​1+y′2​​dx≡∫0x1​​F(y,y′)dx.

Note this is (1.2.2) with refractive index n∝1/yn\propto1/\sqrt{y}n∝1/y​: the brachistochrone is literally a ray of light in a medium whose index falls off as the inverse square root of depth. Fermat and Bernoulli are the same problem.

Reduce. FFF has no explicit xxx, so by Problem 2's Beltrami identity the quantity y′Fy′−Fy'F_{y'}-Fy′Fy′​−F is constant along the solution. Compute it:

Fy′=y′2gy1+y′2,y′Fy′−F=y′2−(1+y′2)2gy1+y′2=−12gy1+y′2. F_{y'} = \frac{y'}{\sqrt{2gy}\sqrt{1+y'^{2}}}, \qquad y'F_{y'}-F = \frac{y'^{2}-\big(1+y'^{2}\big)}{\sqrt{2gy}\sqrt{1+y'^{2}}} = \frac{-1}{\sqrt{2gy}\sqrt{1+y'^{2}}}. Fy′​=2gy​1+y′2​y′​,y′Fy′​−F=2gy​1+y′2​y′2−(1+y′2)​=2gy​1+y′2​−1​.

Setting this equal to −1/2gC-1/\sqrt{2gC}−1/2gC​ for a constant CCC and squaring gives the beautifully compact first integral

y(1+y′2)=C. y\big(1+y'^{2}\big) = C. y(1+y′2)=C.

Integrate. Solve for y′y'y′ and separate:

y′=C−yy⟹dx=yC−y  dy. y' = \sqrt{\frac{C-y}{y}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dd x = \sqrt{\frac{y}{C-y}}\;\dd y. y′=yC−y​​⟹dx=C−yy​​dy.

The substitution that rationalises this is y=C2(1−cos⁡ϑ)=Csin⁡2(ϑ/2)y = \tfrac{C}{2}(1-\cos\vartheta) = C\sin^{2}(\vartheta/2)y=2C​(1−cosϑ)=Csin2(ϑ/2), whence C−y=Ccos⁡2(ϑ/2)C-y = C\cos^{2}(\vartheta/2)C−y=Ccos2(ϑ/2), the square root becomes tan⁡(ϑ/2)\tan(\vartheta/2)tan(ϑ/2), and dy=Csin⁡(ϑ/2)cos⁡(ϑ/2) dϑ\dd y = C\sin(\vartheta/2)\cos(\vartheta/2)\,\dd\varthetady=Csin(ϑ/2)cos(ϑ/2)dϑ. Multiply:

dx=tan⁡ϑ2⋅Csin⁡ϑ2cos⁡ϑ2 dϑ=Csin⁡2ϑ2 dϑ=C2(1−cos⁡ϑ)dϑ. \dd x = \tan\frac{\vartheta}{2}\cdot C\sin\frac{\vartheta}{2}\cos\frac{\vartheta}{2}\,\dd\vartheta = C\sin^{2}\frac{\vartheta}{2}\,\dd\vartheta = \frac{C}{2}\big(1-\cos\vartheta\big)\dd\vartheta. dx=tan2ϑ​⋅Csin2ϑ​cos2ϑ​dϑ=Csin22ϑ​dϑ=2C​(1−cosϑ)dϑ.

Integrating with x=0x=0x=0 at ϑ=0\vartheta=0ϑ=0 and writing a=C/2a=C/2a=C/2:

  x=a(ϑ−sin⁡ϑ),y=a(1−cos⁡ϑ).   \boxed{\;x = a\big(\vartheta-\sin\vartheta\big),\qquad y = a\big(1-\cos\vartheta\big).\;} x=a(ϑ−sinϑ),y=a(1−cosϑ).​

These are the parametric equations of a cycloid — the curve traced by a point on the rim of a wheel of radius aaa rolling along the underside of the horizontal axis. The constant aaa is fixed by requiring the curve to pass through the target point.

Check. For the half-cycloid with a=12a=\tfrac12a=21​, running from the origin to (π/2, 1)(\pi/2,\,1)(π/2,1) and g=9.8g=9.8g=9.8: numerical quadrature gives a descent time of 0.7096 s0.7096\ \mathrm{s}0.7096 s along the cycloid versus 0.8412 s0.8412\ \mathrm{s}0.8412 s along the straight line between the same two points — 16% faster despite being a longer path, because the steep initial drop buys speed early. The first integral y(1+y′2)=Cy(1+y'^{2})=Cy(1+y′2)=C is satisfied to 10−810^{-8}10−8 along the parametric solution.

Problem 2 — the Beltrami identity, and energy arriving early

Suppose L(x,x˙)L(x,\dot x)L(x,x˙) has no explicit dependence on ttt, i.e. ∂L/∂t=0\partial L/\partial t=0∂L/∂t=0. Show that along any solution of the Euler–Lagrange equation the quantity

E  ≡  x˙ ∂L∂x˙−L E \;\equiv\; \dot x\,\pdv{L}{\dot x} - L E≡x˙∂x˙∂L​−L

is constant in time. Then evaluate it for L=12mx˙2−V(x)L=\half m\dot x^{2}-V(x)L=21​mx˙2−V(x) and say what it is.

Solution

Differentiate EEE along the path, using the product rule on the first term:

dEdt=x¨ ∂L∂x˙+x˙ ddt ⁣(∂L∂x˙)−dLdt. \dv{E}{t} = \ddot x\,\pdv{L}{\dot x} + \dot x\,\dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{L}{\dot x}\right) - \dv{L}{t}. dtdE​=x¨∂x˙∂L​+x˙dtd​(∂x˙∂L​)−dtdL​.

The last term is a total time derivative of LLL along the path, which by the chain rule (Chapter 0.6) is

dLdt=∂L∂xx˙+∂L∂x˙x¨+∂L∂t⏟= 0. \dv{L}{t} = \pdv{L}{x}\dot x + \pdv{L}{\dot x}\ddot x + \underbrace{\pdv{L}{t}}_{=\,0}. dtdL​=∂x∂L​x˙+∂x˙∂L​x¨+=0∂t∂L​​​.

Substitute. The x¨ ∂L/∂x˙\ddot x\,\partial L/\partial\dot xx¨∂L/∂x˙ terms cancel between the two lines, and what is left factorises:

dEdt=x˙[ddt ⁣(∂L∂x˙)−∂L∂x]=x˙⋅0=0 \dv{E}{t} = \dot x\left[\dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{L}{\dot x}\right) - \pdv{L}{x}\right] = \dot x \cdot 0 = 0 dtdE​=x˙[dtd​(∂x˙∂L​)−∂x∂L​]=x˙⋅0=0

by (1.2.22). So EEE is conserved. ■\blacksquare■

What it is. For L=12mx˙2−V(x)L=\half m\dot x^{2}-V(x)L=21​mx˙2−V(x) we have ∂L/∂x˙=mx˙\partial L/\partial\dot x=m\dot x∂L/∂x˙=mx˙, so

E=x˙ (mx˙)−(12mx˙2−V)=12mx˙2+V=T+V. E = \dot x\,(m\dot x) - \left(\half m\dot x^{2}-V\right) = \half m\dot x^{2} + V = T+V. E=x˙(mx˙)−(21​mx˙2−V)=21​mx˙2+V=T+V.

The total energy. And notice what the hypothesis was: LLL does not depend explicitly on ttt — that is, the laws are the same today as yesterday. Time-translation symmetry implies energy conservation, and we have just proved the first instance of it without naming it.

Two forward pointers. Chapter 1.4 proves the general theorem — Noether's — of which this is one case among many: every continuous symmetry of the action yields a conserved quantity, with time translation giving energy, spatial translation giving momentum, and rotation giving angular momentum. Chapter 1.3 observes that the combination x˙ ∂L/∂x˙−L\dot x\,\partial L/\partial\dot x - Lx˙∂L/∂x˙−L is exactly the Legendre transform of LLL with respect to x˙\dot xx˙, and renames it the Hamiltonian. Both of those chapters are, in a real sense, this five-line calculation taken seriously.

Caution. EEE is the conserved quantity; it is not always the total energy. It equals T+VT+VT+V only when the relation between generalised and Cartesian coordinates is time-independent (so that TTT is a homogeneous quadratic in q˙\dot qq˙​). Problem 3 supplies a counterexample where EEE is conserved and yet energy demonstrably is not.

Problem 3 — bead on a rotating hoop

A bead of mass mmm slides without friction on a circular hoop of radius RRR, which is held in a vertical plane and driven to rotate about its vertical diameter at a fixed angular velocity Ω\OmegaΩ by a motor. Let θ\thetaθ be the bead's angular position measured from the bottom of the hoop. Find LLL and the equation of motion, identify the effective potential, and find the equilibrium positions and their stability as a function of Ω\OmegaΩ.

Solution

Kinematics. The system has one degree of freedom: the hoop's orientation is dictated by the motor, not by the dynamics, so θ\thetaθ is the only coordinate. The bead's velocity has two orthogonal pieces: motion along the hoop, of magnitude Rθ˙R\dot\thetaRθ˙, and motion carried by the rotation, on a circle of radius Rsin⁡θR\sin\thetaRsinθ about the vertical axis, of magnitude ΩRsin⁡θ\Omega R\sin\thetaΩRsinθ. They are perpendicular, so

T=12m(R2θ˙2+R2Ω2sin⁡2θ),V=−mgRcos⁡θ, T = \half m\Big(R^{2}\dot\theta^{2} + R^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\theta\Big), \qquad V = -mgR\cos\theta, T=21​m(R2θ˙2+R2Ω2sin2θ),V=−mgRcosθ, L=12mR2θ˙2+12mR2Ω2sin⁡2θ+mgRcos⁡θ. L = \half mR^{2}\dot\theta^{2} + \half mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\theta + mgR\cos\theta. L=21​mR2θ˙2+21​mR2Ω2sin2θ+mgRcosθ.

Equation of motion. ∂L/∂θ˙=mR2θ˙\partial L/\partial\dot\theta = mR^{2}\dot\theta∂L/∂θ˙=mR2θ˙ and ∂L/∂θ=mR2Ω2sin⁡θcos⁡θ−mgRsin⁡θ\partial L/\partial\theta = mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin\theta\cos\theta - mgR\sin\theta∂L/∂θ=mR2Ω2sinθcosθ−mgRsinθ, so

  θ¨=sin⁡θ(Ω2cos⁡θ−gR).   \boxed{\;\ddot\theta = \sin\theta\left(\Omega^{2}\cos\theta - \frac{g}{R}\right).\;} θ¨=sinθ(Ω2cosθ−Rg​).​

Effective potential. The Lagrangian has the form 12mR2θ˙2−Veff(θ)\half mR^{2}\dot\theta^{2}-V_{\text{eff}}(\theta)21​mR2θ˙2−Veff​(θ) with

Veff(θ)=−12mR2Ω2sin⁡2θ−mgRcos⁡θ. V_{\text{eff}}(\theta) = -\half mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\theta - mgR\cos\theta. Veff​(θ)=−21​mR2Ω2sin2θ−mgRcosθ.

The rotation has contributed a term to TTT that acts, as far as the θ\thetaθ dynamics is concerned, exactly like a potential — the centrifugal potential. This is where "centrifugal force" comes from without any appeal to fictitious forces: it is a piece of kinetic energy that looks like potential energy because the coordinate it belongs to was eliminated by the motor.

Equilibria. Veff′(θ)=mRsin⁡θ(g−RΩ2cos⁡θ)=0V_{\text{eff}}'(\theta) = mR\sin\theta\big(g - R\Omega^{2}\cos\theta\big) = 0Veff′​(θ)=mRsinθ(g−RΩ2cosθ)=0, giving

θ=0,θ=π,and, if cos⁡θ0=gRΩ2≤1,θ=±θ0. \theta = 0, \qquad \theta = \pi, \qquad\text{and, if } \cos\theta_{0}=\frac{g}{R\Omega^{2}}\le1, \quad \theta=\pm\theta_{0}. θ=0,θ=π,and, if cosθ0​=RΩ2g​≤1,θ=±θ0​.

The last pair exists only when Ω2≥g/R\Omega^{2} \ge g/RΩ2≥g/R. Stability from the second derivative, Veff′′(θ)=−mR2Ω2cos⁡2θ+mgRcos⁡θV_{\text{eff}}''(\theta) = -mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\cos2\theta + mgR\cos\thetaVeff′′​(θ)=−mR2Ω2cos2θ+mgRcosθ:

EquilibriumVeff′′V_{\text{eff}}''Veff′′​Stable?
θ=0\theta=0θ=0 (bottom)mR(g−RΩ2)mR\big(g-R\Omega^{2}\big)mR(g−RΩ2)only if Ω2<g/R\Omega^{2} \lt g/RΩ2<g/R
θ=π\theta=\piθ=π (top)−mR(g+RΩ2)-mR\big(g+R\Omega^{2}\big)−mR(g+RΩ2)never
θ=±θ0\theta=\pm\theta_{0}θ=±θ0​mR2Ω2sin⁡2θ0mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\theta_{0}mR2Ω2sin2θ0​always, where it exists

For the third row, use mgR=mR2Ω2cos⁡θ0mgR = mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\cos\theta_{0}mgR=mR2Ω2cosθ0​ to write Veff′′=−mR2Ω2(2cos⁡2θ0−1)+mR2Ω2cos⁡2θ0=mR2Ω2sin⁡2θ0>0V''_{\text{eff}} = -mR^{2}\Omega^{2}(2\cos^{2}\theta_{0}-1)+mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\cos^{2}\theta_{0} = mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\theta_{0} \gt 0Veff′′​=−mR2Ω2(2cos2θ0​−1)+mR2Ω2cos2θ0​=mR2Ω2sin2θ0​>0.

What this is. As Ω\OmegaΩ is increased past the critical value Ωc=g/R\Omega_{c}=\sqrt{g/R}Ωc​=g/R​, the bottom of the hoop goes from stable to unstable and two new stable equilibria appear symmetrically on either side. The bead must choose one, breaking the left–right symmetry that the equations themselves possess. That is a pitchfork bifurcation, and it is the mechanical prototype of spontaneous symmetry breaking: in Chapter 6.6, VeffV_{\text{eff}}Veff​ becomes the Higgs potential, Ω\OmegaΩ becomes a parameter of the theory, and θ0\theta_{0}θ0​ becomes the vacuum expectation value that gives the WWW and ZZZ their masses. Same picture, same algebra, different letters.

The Problem 2 caution, made concrete. LLL has no explicit ttt, so E=θ˙ ∂L/∂θ˙−L=12mR2θ˙2+Veff(θ)E=\dot\theta\,\partial L/\partial\dot\theta - L = \half mR^{2}\dot\theta^{2} + V_{\text{eff}}(\theta)E=θ˙∂L/∂θ˙−L=21​mR2θ˙2+Veff​(θ) is conserved. But the true energy T+V=12mR2θ˙2+12mR2Ω2sin⁡2θ−mgRcos⁡θT+V = \half mR^{2}\dot\theta^{2}+\half mR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\theta - mgR\cos\thetaT+V=21​mR2θ˙2+21​mR2Ω2sin2θ−mgRcosθ is not: the two differ by mR2Ω2sin⁡2θmR^{2}\Omega^{2}\sin^{2}\thetamR2Ω2sin2θ, which changes as the bead moves. The motor is doing work on the system to hold Ω\OmegaΩ fixed. Conserved and "the energy" are different predicates.

Problem 4 — total derivatives, and the first gauge freedom in this book

Let F(q,t)F(q,t)F(q,t) be any smooth function and define a new Lagrangian

L′  =  L  +  dF(q,t)dt  =  L  +  ∂F∂qq˙+∂F∂t. L' \;=\; L \;+\; \dv{F(q,t)}{t} \;=\; L \;+\; \pdv{F}{q}\dot q + \pdv{F}{t}. L′=L+dtdF(q,t)​=L+∂q∂F​q˙​+∂t∂F​.

Show, in two independent ways, that L′L'L′ gives exactly the same equations of motion as LLL: (a) by looking at what happens to SSS, and (b) by applying the Euler–Lagrange operator to the added term directly. Then say why this matters.

Solution

(a) The action. The added term is a total time derivative, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus (Chapter 0.2) its integral is fixed by the endpoints alone:

S′[q]=∫t1t2 ⁣(L+dFdt)dt=S[q]+F(q(t2),t2)−F(q(t1),t1). S'[q] = \int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\!\left(L + \dv{F}{t}\right)\dd t = S[q] + F\big(q(t_{2}),t_{2}\big) - F\big(q(t_{1}),t_{1}\big). S′[q]=∫t1​t2​​(L+dtdF​)dt=S[q]+F(q(t2​),t2​)−F(q(t1​),t1​).

Every path we compare has the same q(t1)q(t_{1})q(t1​) and q(t2)q(t_{2})q(t2​) — that was the admissibility condition (1.2.4). So the two extra terms take the same value on every admissible path: S′S'S′ and SSS differ by a constant on the entire space of competitors. Adding a constant to a function does not move its stationary points. Hence δS′=δS\delta S'=\delta SδS′=δS and the Euler–Lagrange equations are identical. ■\blacksquare■

(b) Directly. Write G≡dFdt=∂F∂qq˙+∂F∂tG \equiv \dv{F}{t} = \pdv{F}{q}\dot q + \pdv{F}{t}G≡dtdF​=∂q∂F​q˙​+∂t∂F​, and note that GGG is linear in q˙\dot qq˙​ with coefficient ∂F/∂q\partial F/\partial q∂F/∂q, so

∂G∂q˙=∂F∂q⟹ddt∂G∂q˙=ddt ⁣(∂F∂q)=∂2F∂q2q˙+∂2F∂q ∂t. \pdv{G}{\dot q} = \pdv{F}{q} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dv{}{t}\pdv{G}{\dot q} = \dv{}{t}\!\left(\pdv{F}{q}\right) = \frac{\partial^{2}F}{\partial q^{2}}\dot q + \frac{\partial^{2}F}{\partial q\,\partial t}. ∂q˙​∂G​=∂q∂F​⟹dtd​∂q˙​∂G​=dtd​(∂q∂F​)=∂q2∂2F​q˙​+∂q∂t∂2F​.

Meanwhile, differentiating GGG with respect to qqq at fixed q˙\dot qq˙​,

∂G∂q=∂2F∂q2q˙+∂2F∂t ∂q. \pdv{G}{q} = \frac{\partial^{2}F}{\partial q^{2}}\dot q + \frac{\partial^{2}F}{\partial t\,\partial q}. ∂q∂G​=∂q2∂2F​q˙​+∂t∂q∂2F​.

These are equal by the symmetry of mixed partials (Chapter 0.6), so

ddt∂G∂q˙−∂G∂q=0. \dv{}{t}\pdv{G}{\dot q} - \pdv{G}{q} = 0. dtd​∂q˙​∂G​−∂q∂G​=0.

The Euler–Lagrange operator annihilates any total time derivative, identically, for every path — not just on shell. ■\blacksquare■ The two proofs are the same fact seen from opposite ends: (a) says the added term is invisible to the variation, (b) says it is in the kernel of the operator.

Why it matters. The map from Lagrangians to equations of motion is many-to-one. An entire infinite-dimensional family {L+dFdt}\{L + \dv{F}{t}\}{L+dtdF​}, one member for each function F(q,t)F(q,t)F(q,t), describes identical physics. That redundancy has a name: gauge freedom, and this is its first appearance in the book.

It is not an abstraction. ⚑ Quoting forward to Chapter 2.6, the Lagrangian of a particle of charge eee in an electromagnetic field is L=12mx˙2−eφ+e A⋅x˙L = \half m\dot{\vv x}^{2} - e\varphi + e\,\vv A\cdot\dot{\vv x}L=21​mx˙2−eφ+eA⋅x˙, where φ\varphiφ and A\vv AA are the scalar and vector potentials. The fields are unchanged — and so is all measurable physics — under the substitution

A  →  A+∇χ,φ  →  φ−∂χ∂t \vv A \;\to\; \vv A + \nabla\chi, \qquad \varphi \;\to\; \varphi - \pdv{\chi}{t} A→A+∇χ,φ→φ−∂t∂χ​

for any function χ(x,t)\chi(\vv x,t)χ(x,t). Watch what that does to LLL:

L  →  L+e(∂χ∂t+∇χ⋅x˙)=L+e dχdt. L \;\to\; L + e\left(\pdv{\chi}{t} + \nabla\chi\cdot\dot{\vv x}\right) = L + e\,\dv{\chi}{t}. L→L+e(∂t∂χ​+∇χ⋅x˙)=L+edtdχ​.

Exactly a total time derivative. The gauge invariance of electromagnetism is this problem. Chapter 6.3 makes the same observation for a field χ\chiχ that varies independently at each point of spacetime and finds that demanding it generates the electromagnetic field, the strong force and the weak force; Chapter 6.4 is what happens when the gauge parameter is a matrix instead of a number. All of it begins with the observation that dFdt\dv{F}{t}dtdF​ integrates to a boundary term.

The brick you just laid

You can now differentiate with respect to a function. The definition (1.2.9) is Chapter 0.1's, with the displacement hhh promoted to an entire function η\etaη and the derivative promoted to a linear functional; nothing else about the idea changed, which is the dividend for having refused to define the derivative as a slope. From it, in four moves — differentiate under the integral, linearise, integrate by parts, apply the fundamental lemma (which you proved, with a bump function) — comes the Euler–Lagrange equation (1.2.22), one per degree of freedom.

You saw it reproduce Newton exactly, with ∂L/∂x˙\partial L/\partial\dot x∂L/∂x˙ turning out to be the momentum and the whole equation reading p˙=F\dot p = Fp˙​=F. You saw it dispose of constraints by absorbing them into coordinates — and give them back, as multipliers, when you want the constraint force. You proved it keeps its form under any change of coordinates, which F=maF=maF=ma does not, and that is the property that will let physics survive the loss of Cartesian coordinates in Chapter 3. And you saw, honestly, that L=T−VL=T-VL=T−V is a choice justified by results, that "least" is the wrong word, and that the real reason lives in Chapter 5.8.

Where this gets spent. Chapter 1.3 Legendre-transforms this LLL into a Hamiltonian and discovers phase space. Chapter 1.4 acts with symmetries on this SSS and gets Noether's theorem — Problems 2 and the sphere grind box were both previews. Chapters 2.5 and 2.6 write the actions of a relativistic particle and of electromagnetism. Chapter 3.3 replaces the ∫ds\int\dd s∫ds of Worked Example 2 with ∫ds\int\dd s∫ds in curved spacetime and calls the answer gravity; Chapter 3.6 varies the Einstein–Hilbert action and gets the field equations. Chapter 5.2 runs §8's field version in earnest, Chapter 5.8 explains why any of it is true, and Chapters 6.4 and 7.3 write the last two lines of §8.1's table. From here to the end of the book, "solve this theory" will mean "write down its action and vary it".
